story:
Margot sat on her big bed. Her friend Noa had given her a book from daycare. It had a dog on the cover and funny letters inside.

Margot opened the book from the left side. She peeked at a page. "That looks like a stinky sock," she giggled. "Dog, where are you?" The dog was not there. Margot pouted. She sank down into her pillows.

Then Noa's voice popped into her head. "My book opens the other way." Margot turned the book around. She opened it from the right side. There was the dog! "One page, two pages, three!" she said. The dog ran and ran.

Margot grabbed her crayon. She made her own dog on paper. "My dog goes this way," she said. "Your dog goes that way."

"Papa! Look at Noa's funny book!"

Hayden wanted the big blue ball in the library playroom. But the toy box was full of blocks. Too full! Blocks everywhere, blocks on the rug, blocks under the chair.

A girl named Mia started to clean up. "Blocks go in," she said. "Dolls go in. Balls go in." She put in a red block. She put in a sleepy doll. She put in a soft gray elephant. The box got less full.

Then Hayden saw it. When the blocks went in the box, there was room. The loose blocks had made the mess. Now the mess was gone. Hayden picked up the big blue ball. He dropped it in the box, right on top. "Ball goes in!" he said. Mia clapped.

The librarian came over. "The toy box is full," she whispered. "Story time now." Hayden sat down on the big soft rug. He hugged a fluffy pillow that felt like a cloud. The librarian opened a book. Out came a picture of an elephant, and it looked just like the one in the box.

Sarah went to the store with Mom. She wanted a box of crackers. Mom said, "Find aisle ten." Sarah saw a big sign. It had a 1 and a 0. "Why does ten need two numbers?" she asked. Mom said, "Ten is written with a 1 and then a 0." Sarah traced the 1. Then she traced the 0. "I guess ten is special," she said. They walked and counted together. One, two, three steps. Four, five, six steps. Seven, eight, nine. Then ten! They were at the cracker shelf. Sarah saw a cute box with a red triangle on it. "Is this the one?" she asked. Mom nodded. "Yes, that is it." Sarah put it in the cart. The sign said 10 above them. Sarah smiled and waved at the 0.

Hudson put on his shoes. Today was his birthday party. Grandma drove him to the bowling alley.

At the door, his friend Milo was crying. "I thought I would get lost," said Milo. "I did not know where to go."

Hudson had an idea. He pulled out his card. "Look," he said. "My mom drew a map on it. It says the party is here. It says three o'clock, too." Milo stopped crying. He looked at the card. The bowling alley was right there on the paper. "Then I am in the safe place," said Milo. "I came to the right spot!"

Milo's dad was with him, and he smiled. The boys ran to the lanes. Hudson picked a little blue ball. He pushed it down the floor. The ball rolled and rolled. Crash! All the pins fell down. Milo clapped his hands.

The friends ate cake at a big table. Grandma lit the candles, and everyone sang. Hudson blew out the candles in one big puff. "Happy birthday, Hudson!" said Milo, with cake on his nose.

Brooks stood by the big pool. His swim team was in the water. The coach called, "Time to practice kicking!"

Brooks held the wall and kicked his legs. His kicks made waves. The waves made water splash up. One kick, one splash. Kick, splash. Kick, splash.

"When does the season end?" Brooks asked. Mom had the paper with all the games on it. "We can count," she said. They counted the games left. One, two, three. "Three more games," said Mom. "Then the season is done, all the practices and games from start to end."

After practice, Brooks hid his face in his soft towel. It had white sheep on it, like sheep in a snowy field. He peeked out at the pool. "Three more games," he said. "Then I can kick big splashes at every one."

Leah stood at the letter wall at school. Big paper letters hung in a line. But one letter was missing. There was a gap after L.

"Where did M go?" asked her friend Tom.

Tom held the letter M in his hand. "I don't know where it goes," he said. "It slipped off the wall."

Leah tapped her chin. The letters went A, B, C, D, E, F, G. She knew a song about that. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G," she sang. Tom laughed and sang too. "H, I, J, K," they sang together. Then "L, M, N, O, P."

"Stop!" said Leah. "The M comes after the L. I heard it in the song!" The song sang the letters in order from A to Z, and it knew just where M belonged.

Tom handed her the M. The tape was hard to pull off his finger. Leah stuck the M on the wall after the L. It fit just right.

"Now sing it again," said Tom.

"A, B, C, D, E, F, G," they sang, all the way to Z. Miss Bell poked her head in the door. "Is that my singing class?" she said. "You two sound like happy birds."

Leah giggled. "We found where M goes," she said. "The song told us!"

Miss Bell clapped her hands. "Sing it one more time for me," she said. Leah and Tom stood by the wall. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G," they sang, loud and proud.

Edouard ran into the music room. His drum was waiting, but that was not the problem. The problem was the singing game. Everyone had to sing a nursery rhyme from memory, and sing it while clapping.

"What is a nursery rhyme?" Edouard asked his friend Milo.

"It's a short rhyming song," said Milo. "My grandpa taught me one. Twinkle, twinkle, little star."

They tried it together. Edouard clapped too fast, like popping corn. The claps ran away from the words. Milo laughed and fell over sideways.

"Clap like a slow turtle," said Milo.

They clapped. One, two. One, two. Edouard watched his hands. His hands went one, two, and the words went one, two, and they matched! When his claps were slow, the song came out just right.

"Again!" said Edouard. They sang it three more times. Edouard did not forget one single word.

At home, he sang it to his baby brother. His brother clapped his little hands too, one, two, one, two, all the long way to the end.

Brooks stood by the big pool. His swim team lined up on the edge. Coach Sam held a red ball. "Throw it in, then swim fast," Coach Sam said. The sky above was snowy white with soft clouds.

Brooks went first. He threw the ball. It hit the water and went wide. The ball floated far from the ring. Brooks frowned. Then he heard his team. "Try again, Brooks!" they called. "Go, Brooks, go!" They clapped and stomped their feet on the wet tiles.

Brooks sat down on his sheep towel. He hid his face in it for one small minute. Then he peeked out. His team was still cheering. "You can do it," said Mia. Brooks stood up. He threw the ball again. This time it dropped right in the ring. "Hooray!" the team shouted. "Go, Brooks, go!" Brooks laughed and jumped, and his sheep towel flapped like a little white wing.

At school, Willow's class was sorting pictures. Miss Beth put out three big boxes. One box was for animals. One box was for toys. One box was for foods. Willow picked up a picture of a bunny. "The bunny goes with animals," she said. She put it in the animal box. Easy!

Then Ben held up a picture of an apple. "This is a fruit," he said. "It goes in the fruit box." But there was no fruit box. Maya shook her head. "No, it's a food," she said. "It goes in the foods box." Ben frowned. Maya frowned too. Willow looked at the apple picture. It was a fruit. It was also a food. It could be both!

"You can put it in two boxes," Willow said. She held up the apple. "Look. Fruit here. Food here. Same apple." Ben smiled. Maya smiled. Miss Beth gave Willow tape, a safe tool for sticking. Willow taped the apple up between two boxes. It hung there, half in each one. "Both are right," said Ben. "Yay!" said Maya.

Emily wanted a bedtime story. She ran to the shelf. She grabbed a book and held it upside down. "That looks funny," said Daddy. "Try it the other way." Emily turned the book around. Now the letters stood on top. They looked like little curly marks all in a row. She patted the cover. "Start here," said Daddy. He pointed to the front. Emily opened the front cover first.

On the first page were words. Daddy read them out loud. "The moon is up," he read. Emily looked out the window. The moon really was up! "The book told us!" she said. Daddy turned one page at a time. The pages went from front to back. Emily turned some pages herself, slow and careful.

At the end, Daddy closed the back cover. "Again," said Emily. Daddy smiled. "Tomorrow we can read the cereal box, too. It has words on it." Emily remembered the box in the kitchen. Words were everywhere. "And the stop sign!" she said. Daddy kissed her curly head. "Goodnight, Emily." She hugged the book to her chest and closed her eyes.

Sara ran to the park with her bunny. "We will swing high!" she said. But when she got off the swing, bunny was gone. Sara looked in the sand. No bunny. She looked by the slide. No bunny. A big dog barked near the bench. Sara looked there too. Still no bunny.

Then she saw a small wooden box. A sign said Lost and Found. Sara peeked inside. There was a red mitten. There was a thin blue scarf. There was a green cup. One, two, three things, and then, something soft. "Bunny!" Sara shouted. A kind man in a green shirt smiled. "Someone found him and put him in the box," he said. Sara hugged bunny tight. "Park, box, bunny," she sang all the way home. "Found you, found you, found you!"

Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. There were only three little pots.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Grandma. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours."

Leon counted them. "One, two, three," he said. "That is not enough for a rainbow. I am sorry, rainbow."

He dipped his brush in red. He made a red stripe on the paper. Then he put the red brush in the yellow pot.

The paint turned orange. Leon jumped up and down. He mixed yellow and blue next. Green! The green looked like grass.

"Again, again," said Leon. Red, yellow, blue. Mix, mix, mix.

Then he mixed red and blue. Purple! Purple like Grandma's soft scarf.

The orange stripe sank down to dry beside the green one. "Mix, mix, mix," said Leon.

Grandma held the paper up high. It looked like a big ocean wave full of colours.

"My rainbow," said Leon. "One, two, three pots. That was enough after all."

Matteo loved hide-and-seek day at daycare. He found a spot behind the short shelf by the window. He pressed his hands over his eyes. "Now no one can see me," he said.

But Ana walked right up to him. "I see you, Matteo!" she laughed. Matteo peeked through his fingers. Ana was smiling at him. How did she see him? He took his hands away. The room came back. He could see the blocks and the little toy hill on the table. When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you. But Ana still could!

Later, Miss Rosa baked buns in the kitchen. Matteo watched from his chair. He heard the oven door clunk. He smelled warm, sweet bread. He touched his soft sleeve while he waited. Then Miss Rosa gave him a small bun. "Blow on it first," she said. "It is hot, so it could burn your tongue." Matteo blew and blew. He took a little bite. It tasted sweet.

He put his hands over his eyes again. "Can you see me now?" he asked Ana.

"No! You really are hiding," Ana said. Matteo giggled behind his hands.

Benjamin was playing house at daycare. He was the daddy. His friend Mia was the mommy. They had a baby made from a sock.

Then Benjamin dropped the baby sock. It fell on the floor. Mia looked sad. "The baby fell!" she said. Her lip wobbled.

Teacher Ana came over. She picked up the sock. "Look," she said softly. "The sock baby is fine. Socks cannot get hurt." She held it out. "But you can give it a pretend hug."

Benjamin took the sock. He hugged it tight. He rocked it back and forth. "There, there, baby," he said in a small voice. Mia wiped her eyes. Then she laughed.

"Shh, the baby is sleeping," Benjamin whispered. He put the sock on a little bed of blocks. Mia put a tiny blanket on top. It was just a paper napkin, but it looked soft like snow on a mountain.

The baby slept and slept. Benjamin patted it gently. "Time to eat," he said. He held a pretend bottle to the sock. "Mmm," he said.

Then the sock rolled right off the bed! Benjamin grabbed it fast. "I caught you!" he said. He was scared for one second, but then he smiled. The sock could not really be hurt. So he kissed its head and held it close.

"Again, again!" laughed Mia. So Benjamin dropped it, and caught it, and hugged it every time.

Raphael ran to the play room at the community centre. Three big red balls sat by the window. Three tiny yellow beads sat in a cup.

"I want the big group," said Raphael. "The balls look like more."

Mia held out the cup. "You can count them," she said.

Raphael touched each ball. "One, two, three." Then he touched each bead. "One, two, three."

He blinked. "Three and three. They are the same!"

The beads were small, but they counted the same as the big balls. Raphael laughed. He poured the beads into his hand.

Teacher Amy came over with two bowls of crackers. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Raphael counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." He counted the second bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

"This one!" he said. "Six is more than five."

Mia looked at her empty plate. Raphael pushed his bowl toward her.

"You can have some," he said. "Six crackers can be three and three."

Mia smiled and took three crackers. Outside, the snow on the window began to melt in the sun.

"Look," said Raphael. "The snow is melting!"

Axel sat at the dinner table. He wanted pancakes. Daddy made pancakes on Saturday. "How many days until Saturday?" Axel asked.

Mommy held up her hand. "Count with me," she said. Axel tapped her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers. Seven days in one week.

Axel counted again. He poked each finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six." He stopped. One finger was still down. That finger was Saturday! "Six more days, then Saturday!" he shouted.

Axel ran to the calendar. He made a mark on today. Tomorrow he would make another mark. He counted all the marks. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" A whole week on the wall.

At dinner, Axel told his baby sister. "Pancakes on Saturday!" She smiled. One tooth was missing on the bottom. She clapped her hands. Daddy said, "I will not forget the pancakes." Axel ate his peas fast. He made one more mark on the calendar before bed.

Ruby came to Grandma's house after a long drive. Grandma was cooking rice. The pot was hot, so Grandma stirred it herself. Ruby watched from her chair.

Soon the food was on the table. Grandma put a warm, fuzzy wrap around Ruby's shoulders. Then they folded their hands. "Bismillah," said Grandma, before her first bite.

Ruby picked up her spoon. She opened her mouth. Then she stopped. She put the spoon down. "Wait!" said Ruby. She folded her little hands. "Bismillah!" she said, loud and proud.

Grandma clapped her hands. "Yes! You said it first!"

Ruby giggled and took a big bite of rice. One grain stuck to her nose. Grandma laughed and wiped it off.

"My turn again," said Ruby. "Bismillah!" She tapped her empty spoon on the bowl.
"Now there is nothing to eat, silly one," said Grandma.
"Then put more rice," said Ruby.

Luca ran to the backyard. His ball was lost! He wanted to find it before bed.

He looked by the red flowers. He looked by the green grass. He looked up at the blue sky. No ball. Then he heard a bump. The yellow ball rolled out from under a bush. "I found it!" he shouted.

At bedtime, Luca picked socks in his dark room. He could not tell what color they were. He put them on and jumped into bed.

In the morning, the sun came in. Luca looked down. One sock was red. One sock was green. He laughed and laughed. "Silly socks!" he said. He ran outside with the yellow ball, happy to see all the colors in the light.

Maria sat by the big piano. Her teacher, Miss Ada, sat next to her. Maria wanted to play a song all alone. She put her fingers on the keys. The keys were cool and smooth.

Maria played her lion song. It went boom, boom, ROAR! Miss Ada clapped her hands. Maria jumped off the bench and ran to the door. "Wait," said Miss Ada. "Come back, Maria." Maria ran back. "When people clap, you bow," said Miss Ada. She stood up and showed Maria. She bent down low, like a sleepy lion.

The room felt hot from the sun. Maria drank a little water. Then she played her song again. It went boom, boom, ROAR! Miss Ada clapped loud. This time Maria did not run. She bent down low and smiled. She bowed just like a big musician.

"Bravo," said Miss Ada, and she clapped and clapped.

Avery went to the store with Dad. The store was bright and cold. Avery wanted a big red apple. She reached up and grabbed for it. Dad put her hand down. "We say please when we ask for something," he said.

Avery looked at the apple. She put her hands behind her back. "Apple, please," she said. Dad smiled and picked one out. He put it in the bag. Avery held the bag with two hands.

At the bread table, a boy grabbed for a bun. His mom shook her head. The boy stopped. Then he said, "Bun, please." His mom gave him the bun. Avery watched the whole thing. Grab did not work. Please worked.

In the cart, Avery sat on the soft seat like a pillow. She hugged the bag. "My apple, please, I asked," she said. At the checkout, they waited for their turn. Then it was their turn. Dad paid. Avery carried her apple out the door. "Apple, please," she said one more time. Dad laughed. "Apple, all yours," he said.

Violet got to daycare. It was morning. Sun sat on the little red table. Her friend Leo was already there.

Teacher Mia said, "Snack time is soon." Violet sat down on the rug. She waited. "Is it now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Teacher Mia. "Soon means in a little while."

Violet watched the class. Kids built a tall block tower. A boy poured cold water into the paint cups. The water went splash, splash. The tower fell down with a big sound. Everyone laughed.

"Now snack?" asked Violet. "Almost," said Teacher Mia. Violet looked out the window. A bird hopped on the fence. One hop. Two hops. Then the bird flew away.

"Snack time now," said Teacher Mia. She poured cold milk into small cups. Violet got crackers and apple slices. "It came!" said Violet. "Soon was just a little while."

Yesterday Violet had missed snack. Tomorrow she would not miss it. Today she held her cup with two hands.

"Yesterday, today, tomorrow," said Leo. "Now we eat." Violet took a big bite of her apple. "Later we go outside," she said. "And that is soon too."

Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house today. Yesterday they could not go. It rained yesterday. "Grandma has a surprise for you," said Mama. "When?" asked Paisley. "Not now. We drive now. We get there later." Paisley looked out the window. She saw a wild bird fly by. Then the bird made a tree shake. Leaves fell down. One thing made another thing happen. Paisley tapped the window. "Bird, leaf, fall," she said. Mama smiled. "Grandma has baby chicks," said Mama. "One chick came out of its egg this morning." Paisley held up her hand. She counted days on her fingers. "Today, then one, two, three, four, five," she said. She ran out of fingers. "Mama! My hand is not big enough!" "A week has seven days," said Mama. "Use your other hand too." Paisley put up two more fingers. "Seven! I did it!" The car stopped. Grandma opened the door. In her hands was a small yellow chick. "Hello, little one," said Paisley.

James ran into the writing club room. His friend Mila was already there. A big basket of pencils sat on the table.

"Today we write our names!" said Miss Ana. She handed James a fat pencil. He gripped it in his fist. Miss Ana showed him how to pinch it near the tip. "Like this," she said. James pinched it too.

He drew a big J. Then an A. Then an M. The M had all straight lines. So did the L and the S. Wait, the S was not straight. The S had curves!

"My M and L are straight," said James. "But my S and O are curvy!" He sorted his letters into two piles. The straight ones sat on the left. The curvy ones sat on the right.

"The O is all round," said Mila. "Like a ball!"

James pressed his pencil down. The straight lines were easy. The curves were hard. He made a wobbly O. Then another O. The next one was round.

He held up his paper. His full name sat on the page. "I did it!" he said. Miss Ana clapped. James popped out of his chair to show Mila.

"Look at my O!" he said. "It has curves, just like yours."

Chloe held Mommy's hand at the store door. She wanted a red apple for her snack. But first they had to cross the big road.

The light was red. "Red means stop," said Mommy. The cars stopped. Then the light turned green. "Green means go!" said Chloe. The cars went, and they walked too.

Inside the store, Chloe saw yellow bananas and green lettuce. She put three apples in the bag. The bag was heavy, so Mommy helped carry it.

At the door, a little boy was crying. His toy pig had fallen on the floor. Chloe picked it up and gave it back. The boy smiled.

Outside, the light was red again. "Stop!" said Chloe. They waited, and her apple waited too, safe in the bag.

Ivy sat in the waiting room. Her teddy bear was lost somewhere at home. "Where did he go?" she asked Mom. "Maybe under your bed," said Mom. "But my room is dark," said Ivy.

The nurse came out. "Time to see Doctor Lee," she said. Doctor Lee smiled. "Let's check your eyes," she said. Ivy looked at a chart with her eyes. She could see the big letters. Then Doctor Lee rang a tiny bell. Ivy heard it with her ears. She sniffed a cotton ball with her nose. "I smell nothing," she said. "Good," said Doctor Lee. "Your tongue tastes, and your fingers touch." Ivy held out her hand. Doctor Lee touched it gently. "You are a healthy team," she said. The grumpy old man in the corner waited too, and Ivy waited with him, nice and quiet.

At home, the sun had gone down. Ivy stood at her dark bedroom door. She could not see the bed. She could not see teddy. Mom reached up and turned on the lamp. Light filled the room. Then Ivy saw him! Teddy was under the bed, just where Mom said. Ivy picked him up and hugged him tight. "Found you," she said.

Brielle got to school early. The table had pencils and paper. Today she would write her name.

"Make a B first," said Ms. Amy. Brielle gripped the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard. The B looked like a potato.

Then it was time to line up. Brielle ran with her pencil up high. The point waved near Ben's nose. Ben jumped back.

Brielle stopped. She looked at the point. She turned it down by her side. She walked slowly to the rug.

Ms. Amy smiled. "Nice walking," she said.

Brielle went back to the table. She held the pencil with her fingers, not her fist. She made a B. Then an R. "It looks like a real B!" said Ben.

Brielle counted her letters. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." B-R-I-E-L-L-E.

"That is my whole name," said Brielle. "It is not a joke. It is real."

James ran into the writing club with his big sister's pet rabbit soft toy under his arm. He sat down fast. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

Miss Ana gave him a pencil. She showed him how to hold it. "Pinch it like this," she said. James pinched the pencil. He drew a J, then an A. He drew an S, then an M. Then he stopped and looked. "J-A-S-M-E? That looks funny," he said. His friend Lily slid the name card over to him. James looked at the card. The letters were J-A-M-E-S. He erased two letters. He wrote them back the right way. "Now it says James!" he shouted. "It popped into place!"

Miss Ana clapped. James held up his paper. "Look, rabbit!" he said. "Your friend has a full name on my page." Then he started on a new paper right away. "I'm making another one," he said.

Ibrahim woke up in his little bed. The sun was up too. Mama said, "Morning time! We brush our teeth in the morning." Ibrahim brushed up and down. One, two, three, spitting bubbles in the sink. Then Mama helped him get dressed. One sock, two socks, good warm feet.

At breakfast Ibrahim ate eggs and toast. He heard a pop from the stove. "That is the fire under the pan," said Mama. "I will cook. You stay back." Ibrahim stayed back and watched.

Night came. Ibrahim had a bath with bubbles. He heard the water go drip, drip, drip. He put on his soft pajamas. He got into bed and pulled the cover up. Then he sat up fast. "Mama! My teeth!" He ran to the sink and brushed, one, two, three. "Good job," said Mama. Ibrahim grinned and showed his clean teeth.

Mila packed her little red backpack. She put in her teddy bear, Dot. "We are going camping," said Mama. "First we ride in a big plane."

At the airport, Mila saw a long line. People put their bags on a moving belt. The bags went into a big machine. The machine has a little tunnel, like a cave for bags.

Mila put her backpack on the belt. It slid away. It went into the tunnel. Then it was gone!

"My Dot!" cried Mila. "Where is my Dot?"

Daddy knelt down beside her. "Watch the belt," he said. "Just watch."

Mila watched and watched. Then, pop! Her backpack came out the other end. It slid right down to her. Mila opened the top. Dot was inside, safe and soft.

"Dot went through the machine," said Mila. She hugged Dot tight. "Dot came out the other end!"

The security man at the desk smiled at her. Mila stood tall and proud. She carried her backpack all by herself onto the plane.

Later, at the campsite, Mila put Dot on her pillow. "You went in a machine," she whispered. "And you came out the other end."

Dot sat still, in the tent.

Raphael was at the community centre. The sun came in the big window. He sat on the floor with his friend Mia.

"I have more blocks," said Mia.
"No, I have more," said Raphael.

They both wanted the red blocks. Miss Jo said, "Try lining them up."

So they did. One block here. One block there. One across from one. They counted as they went. "One, two, three, four, five." Raphael's row was longer. His row had blocks left over.

"See? You have more," said Mia. She looked a little sad.

Raphael pushed two blocks across the floor. "Now we both have five," he said.

Then something fell. It was an ice cube, and it began to melt on the warm floor.

"Who put an ice cube there?" asked Raphael.

Mia laughed. "It was me. It was a surprise. My hands were hot!"

Raphael touched the wet spot. The ice cube had turned to water. Not broken. Just water.

"Let's get ten blocks," said Raphael. "Then we can line them all up."

"Ten blocks, one long row," said Mia. "Let's count."

"One, two, three," said Raphael, and they counted on and on.

Maria put on her new hat. She ran out to the backyard. "Papa, I want to see the pot!" she said. Papa was cooking corn on the grill. The pot sat on top. Maria took one big step. Then another big step.

"Stop there," said Papa. "The pot makes steam. Steam is hot and can burn. We stay back." Maria stopped. She put her hands behind her back. The pot went bubble, bubble, bubble. White steam rose up, up, up. "I see the bubbles!" said Maria. "I see them from here!"

The steam floated away like a little cloud. Maria watched it go. Papa gave her a towel. She helped him wipe the table, far from the hot pot. Papa counted to ten while the corn cooked. Maria counted too. Then Papa carried the pot away. He put warm corn on Maria's plate. Maria touched the plate with one finger. It was just right. "Good waiting," said Papa. Maria smiled under her new hat.

Hazel put her teddy bear on the picnic table. "This is my library," she said. She lined up her books in little rows. The animal books sat together. The toy books sat together. The food books sat together.

Rabbit hopped by and stopped. Rabbit wanted a book about animals. Hazel looked at her rows. She went straight to the animal row. There was a book with a bunny on the cover. "Here you go," said Hazel. Rabbit made a happy sound, a little thump on the grass.

Then Hazel heard a small chirp. A bird wanted a book too. Hazel looked and looked. Which row? The bird was an animal. So she patted the animal row. There was a book with a blue bird on it. The bird pecked the cover gently, then flew up with the pages flapping. "Books fly home at my library," said Hazel.

Maria put on her new hat and went to the backyard. Grandma was at the little grill table. A kettle sat on the grill, and it began to hum. Maria wanted to see the bubbles inside. "Can I look?" she asked.

"Come stand by me," said Grandma. "The steam is hot. We stay back." Maria stood next to Grandma's legs. She held on to Grandma's apron. The kettle went psssss. White steam floated up, up, up. Maria reached out one finger. Grandma caught her hand right away. "Hot," said Grandma. "We stay back."

Maria pulled her hand back. She stayed close to Grandma. They watched the steam together. The kettle began to sing. Grandma put on a big glove and lifted the kettle. Then Grandma poured warm water into a cup. Maria helped wipe the table with a small cloth. "All clean," said Maria. Grandma smiled and patted her new hat. The steam had gone up, up, up, and away.

Bennett went to Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming. Grandma said, "We need to get ready."

Bennett found a big box. He cut the tape with safety scissors. Grandma held the box steady. Inside were diapers. Small ones. So many diapers.

"Why so many?" Bennett asked.

"We will see," said Grandma.

Then baby Rose came home. Bennett watched. Rose drank her milk. Then Rose made a wet diaper. Grandma changed it. One diaper in the basket.

Rose drank more milk. Another wet diaper. Two diapers in the basket.

"Again?" said Bennett.

"Again," said Grandma. "She is too little for the toilet."

Bennett counted the diapers. One, two, three, four. The basket got full. Bennett felt a little sad. The diapers were going too fast.

Then Grandma gave him a job. "Draw a picture for Rose," she said. Bennett took his pencil. He drew a big happy baby. He drew a big stack of diapers too.

Rose looked at the picture. Rose waved her small hand.

"Hello, Rose," said Bennett. "I will count your diapers every day."

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. She was going to get a fuzzy new toothbrush. But first, the nurse said Grace could pick a sticker.

"I want the ice cream sticker," said Grace. She reached out her hands. Then she saw them. There was glitter glue on her fingers from the waiting room.

"The glitter can hide in the little lines on your hands," said the nurse. "Let's wash it off."

At the little sink, Grace scrubbed fast. The glitter stayed. She scrubbed again, fast fast fast. Still it stayed.

The nurse began to sing. "Happy birthday to you." Grace sang too. They sang it all the way through, and Grace kept scrubbing.

Grace looked down. Her hands were shiny and clean. "The song made my washing long," she said.

The nurse smiled and gave her the sticker. Grace held it up to the light.

Leah stood by the classroom door and looked at the big alphabet chart. Her teacher, Mrs. Park, was writing letters on the board.

"Leah, can you find the letter S?" asked Mrs. Park.

Leah found it. "S goes sss," she said, wiggling like a snake. Ben laughed next to her.

Then Leah looked at the chart again. There were so many letters. She wanted to count them. She touched A. "One," she said. She touched B. "Two." She kept going, all the way down the row.

"Twenty-six!" she shouted. "Twenty-six letters, all in a row!"

"That many?" said Ben. "Count again. I don't believe it."

Leah counted again. She did not slip up. "Twenty-six," she said again.

So Mrs. Park had an idea. "Let's find a letter for each friend," she said. "When I say your name, say the first sound."

"Ben," said Mrs. Park.

"Buh, buh, Ben!" said Ben.

"Leah," said Mrs. Park.

"Luh, luh, Leah!" said Leah. Then she ran to the chart and put her finger on L.

"Hard to believe we all fit," said Ben, counting the kids.

The bell rang. Leah waved at the chart on her way out. "Bye, twenty-six letters," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He wanted to toss a beanbag right into it.

He threw the beanbag overhand, high from his shoulder. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed far away with a little sound, tap.

"Why did it go so far?" Hudson asked.

"Try it like this," said Ms. Kim. She held her beanbag down low. Then she swung her arm forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop.

Hudson picked up his beanbag. He held it down low by his knees. He swung his arm forward and up. The beanbag went up, then down. Plunk! It landed in the hoop.

"I did it!" said Hudson.

Next, his friend Ben rolled him a big blue ball. The first time, it bounced off his hands and the floor got messy with scattered cones. Hudson tried again. He held out both hands and pulled the ball in close. He caught it!

"Nice catch," said Ben.

Hudson tossed his beanbag one more time. Low, forward, up, plunk. He grinned and jumped.

Billie went to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on her face. Dad sat on a bench by the big tree.

Billie ran to the slide. She put her hand on it. The slide felt hot. "Ouch," she said. She pulled her hand back fast. Dad came over. He poured some water on the slide. Then the slide felt cool. Billie slid down. Whee!

Next Billie saw a tall fence at the far end. A shiny bottle sat by the fence. She wanted to look at it. But she looked back at the bench. She could not see Dad. The tree was too far away. Billie could not see Dad, so Dad could not see her. She ran back to the bench. "There you are," said Dad.

"I could not see you," said Billie. Dad held her hand. They walked back together. Dad picked up the bottle with a bag. "Not for touching," he said.

Then they sorted the leaves by the swing. Big ones here, small ones there. A lazy bee buzzed by. Billie watched it land on a flower. "Time for school soon," said Dad. Billie slid down one more time. The slide was still cool.

Anna wanted to find her toy robot. It was lost somewhere in the house. She looked with her eyes. She listened with her ears. She heard a little beep. Was it under the bed? Yes! The robot was there, covered in dust.

Anna pulled the robot out. Some dust flew up. She blinked and blinked. The dust did not get in her eyes. Her eyelashes caught it. She touched her eyelashes with her fingers. "They are like tiny gates," she thought. "Where does the dust go if I blink?" It went away. Her eyes stayed clean.

Then Anna smelled cookies with her nose. Daddy had baked them. She tasted one. It was sweet and warm. She touched the warm plate, very carefully. "Found you, robot!" she said. She hugged him tight. The robot beeped a happy beep.

Ruby and Mama drive to Grandma's house. Grandma hugs Ruby at the door. "Lunch is ready," says Grandma. There is bread, soup, and a fuzzy peach for later.

Ruby climbs into her little chair. She picks up her spoon. She is about to take a big bite. Then she stops. Wait. Something comes first. She forgot!

"Grandma, what do we say first?" asks Ruby.

"Bismillah," says Grandma. "It means in the name of God."

Ruby puts down her spoon. She takes a breath. "Bismillah!" she says, loud and proud. Grandma claps. "There you go," says Grandma. Now Ruby takes her big bite. The soup is warm and good.

After lunch, Ruby yawns. "Nap time," says Grandma, and she spreads a soft blanket. Ruby lies down and holds the fuzzy peach. "Bismillah," she whispers to it, just one more time.

Elijah went to the ice rink with Mom and his friend Sam. They skated on the fresh ice until their toes were cold. Then they sat on a bench with hot cocoa. A big soccer game was on the TV by the snack bar.

Elijah watched a player run with the ball. The player kicked it high. The ball went up over the net. The crowd made a sad sound. "He missed," said Sam.

Elijah kept watching. He waited a long time. Another player ran fast. She kicked the ball low. The ball rolled along the ground. It went right into the net. The crowd jumped up and cheered.

The goal! Elijah stood on the bench and waved his arms. "The ball went in!" he said. Sam kissed his own hand and patted the screen. Mom laughed. A new player got the ball. Elijah sat very still and watched. His eyes followed the ball the whole way. It went into the net again. "Goal!" said Elijah.

Rowan wanted to make cookies. Mama mixed the dough in a big round bowl. Rowan got the cookie cutters. One was a circle. One was a square. One was a triangle.

Rowan pressed the circle cutter down. "Look, a circle cookie!" he said. Then he wanted to cut the circle cookie into two little cookies. He looked for a corner to start cutting. He looked and looked. He turned the cookie over. There was no corner anywhere. "Where is the corner?" he said. Mama laughed. "Look again," she said. Rowan ran his finger all around the edge. Round and round and round. No corner, not one.

Rowan picked up the square cookie instead. He felt its corners. One, two, three, four! He cut it from corner to corner. Two triangles fell apart on the table. "I did it!" said Rowan.

Mama put the cookies in the oven. Rowan waited by the closed oven door. He sang a little song while he waited. Then the cookies came out, and there was a small surprise. The circle cookie had puffed up like a little pillow, round on top too. No corners up there either. Rowan took a bite of his triangle. "Best cookies ever," said Mama. Rowan grinned and sang his song again.

Hailey sat in the cafe with her mama. Mama gave her a pencil and a paper napkin. "Can you write your name?" asked Mama.

Hailey grabbed the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out big and wobbly. An H looked like a ugly little squiggle. "Mine looks wrong," said Hailey. Her lip went down, almost ready to cry.

Mama sat close. She kissed the top of Hailey's head. Then she showed her hand. She pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. Hailey tried it. Pinch and rest. Pinch and rest. The pencil felt light in her hand now.

Hailey drew an H. It stood up tall. Then an A, then an I. The pencil made neat little lines. "Look, Mama!" said Hailey. Her whole name sat on the napkin, letter by letter, small and clear.

Josephine wanted to move the big red box. It was full of blocks. She pulled it. It did not move. She pulled again. Still, it stayed. "It is so heavy," she said.

Her teacher, Miss Amy, smiled. "Try the pillow instead," she said. Josephine picked up the small feather pillow. It went up in her hands. It was light! She carried it fast across the room. Then she went back to the box. She carried one block at a time, slow and steady. Drop, tap, drop, tap. Soon the box was empty.

Now Josephine picked up the box. It felt light in her arms. "Heavy and light are opposites," said her friend Milo. Josephine hugged the box and carried it to the window. The sun made warm spots on the floor. She set the box down and gave it a kiss. "My light box," she said.

Charlie got to school and saw a big yellow pencil on his table. Today he would write his name! He grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard. The letters came out wobbly. The C looked like a squiggle.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Watch me," she said. She pinched the pencil between her thumb and her first finger. Then she let it rest on her middle finger. "Now you try. Pinch, then rest."

Charlie pinched the pencil with his thumb and first finger. He rested it on his middle finger. The pencil did not slip. He wrote a C. Then an H. Then A. Then R. He lifted the pencil and looked. "Charlie! It says Charlie!" He wrote it again and again, all down the road of paper.

"Look, Miss Rosa!" said Charlie. "My hand did it!"

Milan loved the school library. On Tuesday his teacher said, "Yesterday we read about bears. Tomorrow we will go to the library."

Milan could not wait. He wanted the bright red book about trucks.

On Wednesday morning, Milan asked his friend Sam, "Is today the library day?"

Sam said, "I don't know."

Milan asked his teacher. She smiled and said, "Yes. Today is the day. It is happening right now."

Milan jumped up and down. "Now?" he asked.

"Now," said the teacher. "But first we will cook bread in the kitchen. The library comes later."

Milan waited. He stirred the flour. He watched the teacher put the pan in the oven, because the oven was hot. The bread smelled good.

"Now is it later?" Milan asked.

"Not yet," said the teacher.

Milan waited some more. Then the teacher said, "Now it is later. Time to go."

Milan held his coin for the library pot. He found the bright red truck book. He sat down and turned the first page.

Mateo sat in the car seat. He held his soft blue bunny. Then the car went over a bump. Bunny jumped out of his hands. Bunny was gone.

"Bunny!" said Mateo. He looked down. He looked under the seat. It was too dark. He could not see anything at all. "Oh no," he said. "Bunny is alone down there."

Daddy stopped the car at the store. The store would sell bread and milk. Daddy looked back. "What is wrong?" he asked.

"I lost Bunny," said Mateo. "It is dark under the seat. I cannot see."

Daddy reached into the glove box. He took out a little flashlight. He clicked it on. The light was bright and yellow. "Here," said Daddy. "Try this."

Mateo pointed the flashlight under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore. The light made it bright. And there was Bunny! Bunny was sitting by a tissue and a cracker.

"Bunny!" Mateo shouted. He reached down. He grabbed Bunny's soft ear. He pulled him up fast. "I found you!" he said. He hugged Bunny tight. Bunny's fur touched Mateo's hair.

Daddy laughed. "Good helper, that light," he said.

Mateo held Bunny and the flashlight together. "Now we can find anything," said Mateo. "Anything at all!" He clicked the light on and off. On and off. "Let's go, Daddy. Let's go buy bread!"

Jasper stood by his bed. He wanted to go to Mia's house. He wanted to go now.

"Now we eat lunch," said Mom. "Later we sleep. Tomorrow we go to Mia."

Jasper made a sad face. "Sorry, buddy," said Mom. "Tomorrow is the day after today."

Jasper looked at his window. He saw the sun up high. He saw his small bed. He touched his pillow, one pat, two pats, three pats.

"Now I sleep?" he asked.

"After lunch," said Mom. Jasper ate his carrots. He kept his shoes by the door, ready.

Then he slept, and slept, and slept. The sun went away. The sun came back.

"Is it today now?" Jasper asked.

"It is today," said Mom. "And yesterday we got ready. So now we go!"

Jasper grabbed his shoes. "Mia's teacher can see my truck!" he said.

He ran to the door.

Evan was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big red rug with letters on it. Evan wanted to find every letter he knew.

"Look, Grandma! A B!" he said. Then he saw another letter. It looked the same. It looked different. It was shy, hiding its face.

"Grandma, this word says bog!" Evan read. Then he laughed. "Bog! That is a funny word!"

Grandma laughed too. Evan got down on his knees. He looked very close. One round part faced left. One round part faced right.

"It is not bog," Evan said. "It is dog! The dog lives next door!"

Grandma found a feather by the door. Evan used the feather to point. "B goes this way," he said. "D goes that way!"

He pointed at the letters again and again. "This way! That way! This way!" Then Evan jumped up.

"Grandma, I can read dog! Let's find more words!"

Sadie sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. Her brother Ben sat next to her. He had a small red puzzle in his hands.

Ben dropped the puzzle. It fell under the seat. "Oh no," said Ben. "My puzzle fell. Please help me, Sadie."

Sadie reached down. She reached slowly. She reached again. At last she got the puzzle. "Here you go," she said.

"Thank you, Sadie," said Ben.

Sadie did not know what to say. She looked out the window. She waited. She thought and thought.

Then Mommy said, from the front seat, "You're welcome, Ben."

Sadie looked at Mommy. Then she looked at Ben. "You're welcome!" said Sadie.

Ben smiled a big smile. Mommy read the road signs out loud. "That was cool," said Ben. He gave Sadie a little pat on her hand.

At the next stop, Mommy turned around. "Can you pass me the map, please?" she asked.

Sadie passed the map. "Thank you, Sadie," said Mommy.

"You're welcome!" said Sadie, loud and clear. The car went on, and Sadie sang all the way home.

Paisley wanted a bedtime story. She ran to her room. Her big book sat on the bed.

She picked it up. She opened it. The pages were all mixed up. The bear came before his house. The dog came before his ball. "That is funny," said Paisley.

Mama sat down next to her. "You opened the back cover," Mama said. "Try the front." Paisley turned the book over. She found the shiny front cover. She opened it there.

Now the bear found his house. Now the dog found his ball. One page, then the next page. Paisley turned each page herself. The story went in order, all the way to the end.

The last page showed the bear asleep. Paisley gave a big yawn.

"Read it again tomorrow," said Mama. "From the front."

"From the front," said Paisley, and pulled up her blanket.

Brooklyn stood at the bus stop with Mom. The wind blew. Brooklyn put her arms in her furry coat. One arm in. One arm out. She tried again. One arm in. One arm in. Both arms were in!

Now the zipper. Brooklyn held the little silver tab. Up, up, up. It stuck. She waited. She tried again. Up, up, up. Click, click, zip! The coat was closed. Mom smiled. "You did it all by yourself."

Yesterday was different. Brooklyn had dropped her coat on the floor. It went under a chair. She looked and looked. She could not find it. "Where is my coat?" she asked. Today she put it on the hook by the door. The hook held it up high.

The bus came. "I can dream of carrots on the bus," said Brooklyn. "Rabbit dreams are the best." Mom laughed. Brooklyn climbed the steps, warm in her zipped coat.

Milo got to school with a red apple in his bag. He waved to his teacher, a kind woman with a loose paint smock. "Today we paint," she said. "We paint after nap time."

Milo loved to paint cats. He thought about his cat all morning. He built with blocks. He ate his apple. Then it was time to rest.

Milo slept on his little blue mat. When he woke up, the light felt soft and yellow. "It is morning," he said. "I missed the painting!"

His teacher shook her head and smiled. "No, Milo. Look outside." The sun was low in the sky. "It was morning before your nap. Now it is afternoon."

Milo looked out the window. The sun sat behind the trees. It was afternoon, and the painting table was open.

"Today is still today!" said Milo. He paid close attention to his brush. He painted a big orange cat, all the way until the light grew dim.

Declan loved the sand table at daycare. It was warm and soft. It ran through his fingers like sugar.

"I want sand now," said Declan.

"Sand play was yesterday," said Miss Jo. "Today we paint. Sand play comes tomorrow."

Declan had a problem. Tomorrow felt far away. "Where did yesterday go?" he asked.

"It went when you slept," said Miss Jo.

At nap time, Declan lay on his little cot. The blanket was soft. He closed his eyes. He slept.

When he woke up, the room looked different. Miss Jo pointed at the sand table. "Now it is today," she said.

Declan touched the warm sand. It stuck to his fingers. He made a tall sand cake.

"Yesterday I painted," said Declan. "Today is sand!"

"Tomorrow we paint again," said Miss Jo. Declan smiled and patted the cake flat.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He had a big pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. "R-y-a-n," said the librarian, Miss Kim. Ryan held the pencil tight. He began at the right side of the page. He made an R. Then a Y. Then the pencil slid off the paper. There was no more room! Ryan frowned like he had tasted something sour. "My A won't fit," he said. Miss Kim sat down next to him. "Try the other side," she said. Ryan thought for a minute. He put his pencil down at the left edge. R. Y. A. N. All four letters fit on one line! Ryan smiled big. "Look, Miss Kim! My whole name!" He wrote it again, left to right, one more time.

Alice sat in her car seat. Today they were going to Grandma's house. The wheels went round and round on the road.

Alice wanted to see Grandma now. "Are we there yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "We will get there later. First we drive, then we arrive."

Alice looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. The car went past, and the cow got small and small. Alice put her finger on the window. "Bye, cow."

Yesterday Alice had packed her small red bag. The bag was heavy with her teddy bear. Mom had helped her lift it into the car. Tomorrow Grandma would make pancakes. But how long was tomorrow?

Alice held up one hand. She counted her fingers. One for today. One for tomorrow. She wanted to count a whole week. "A week has seven days," said Mom. Alice counted. One, two, three, four, five. Her hand ran out of fingers.

"I need more fingers!" Alice said. She looked at her other hand. She opened it wide and counted on. Six, seven. There. A whole week filled two hands.

The car turned a corner. A red gate came into view. Grandma was waving by the door.

"Grandma!" Alice called. "I counted a week with my fingers!"

"Well," said Grandma, "come and tell me all about it."

Milo loved the red blocks at school. He wanted to build a tall tower. But today the blocks were busy. A girl named Ana was using them.

"Can I have the blocks now?" Milo asked.

Miss Ella, the teacher, shook her head. "You can have them later," she said. "Ana is using them now."

Milo sat down at the table. He waited. He drew a cat. He looked up. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Ella.

Milo drew a sun next to the cat. He heard Ana stack a block. Click, click, click. He looked up again. "Is it later yet?"

"Not yet," said Miss Ella. "Later means some time after now. Not right away."

So Milo kept drawing. He paid attention to his cat. He gave the cat a long tail.

Soon Ana stood up. "I am done," she said. "You can have the blocks now."

Milo ran to the carpet. He stacked the red blocks. One, two, three, four. The tower was as tall as his chin. Then Milo laughed. Later had come, and he had not even noticed.

A woman from the office walked by. She smiled at the tall tower. "Tomorrow you can build it again," she said.

"Tomorrow is after today," said Milo. "Right now I have blocks."

Ana sat down next to him. She put one more block on top. "Later we can paint," she said.

"Now we build," said Milo.

Charlie ran to the little table at school. Today he would write his name! Ms. Rose gave him a fat pencil. "Hold it like this," she said. Charlie gripped it tight. He pressed down hard. The pencil slid off the paper. The C came out all wobbly. "Yucky," Charlie said. "My C looks like a squiggle."

Ms. Rose smiled. "Try sorting your letters first," she said. She gave him two roads of paper. One road was for straight letters. One road was for curvy letters. Charlie picked up the C. It had a big curve. He put it on the curvy road. He picked up the L. Straight lines, top to bottom! He put it on the straight road. A, H, L, straight. C and R, curvy. "Two curvy, three straight!" he said.

Now Charlie knew his letters. He lifted his pencil and went slow. Straight lines for L, easy peasy. The C took a big round curve, round like a ball. One letter, two letters, three letters, four, five, six, seven. "Charlie!" he shouted. "I did it! My name is on the paper!" He lifted the paper up high. "Look, Ms. Rose! Look at my road of letters!"

Zoe sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a magic dragon. The dragon would be red, like fire.

Zoe picked up her brush. She dipped it in the red paint. She painted the dragon's long tail. Then she wanted yellow wings. She dipped the brush in the yellow pot.

The yellow came out all pink and muddy. Zoe frowned. Her yellow wings looked wrong. The red had jumped into the yellow!

Zoe put her brush in the water cup. She swished it round and round. The water turned pink. Then she counted to three, like a game. She dipped the brush in the yellow again.

Now the yellow was bright as the sun. Zoe painted big yellow wings. Then she swished the brush again, and dipped it in the blue pot. Yellow and blue touched on the paper.

A green spot grew. It looked like a leaf from a magic tree. Zoe clapped her hands.

Tom leaned over from the next seat. "Can I have a turn with the magic water?"

"Yes," said Zoe, in her polite dragon-queen voice. "Swish first. Then the colours stay clean."

Tom swished his brush. His paint stayed bright too. Together they painted a green forest for the dragon to fly over.

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He wanted to write his name all by himself. His brother could write his name already. But Max was too young for big kid school, and his letters came out wobbly.

"How do the letters get straight?" Max asked.

Grandma gave him a paper. It had dotted letters on it. The dots made the shape of M-A-X. Grandma held the pencil in his hand. She showed him where his fingers should go.

Max pushed the pencil along the dots. The pencil made a line. The line went right over the dots! He traced the M. He traced the A. He traced the X. Each dotted letter turned into a dark, solid letter.

"Look what I made!" Max said.

Grandma put the paper up on the fridge to dry. Max ran to get more paper. "Can I do my name again?" he asked. "One more time, then two more times!"

Jaxson ran to the table. His hands were dirty with mud. "Snack time!" he called. Mama looked at his hands. She shook her head. "Hands first," she said. She pointed to the sink.

Jaxson went to the sink. He turned the cold tap. The water felt cool and smooth. He rubbed the soap. One hand, two hands. Bubbles grew big and white. The mud went down the drain. He watched it swirl away. "Bye, mud," he said.

Now his hands were clean. He ran back to the table. He picked up his apple slice. It crunched in his mouth. Mama smiled. The baby girl in her high chair banged her spoon. "Ba!" she said.

Later Jaxson played in the bath. The water was warm. His rubber duck floated by. After the bath, he put on his soft pajamas. One leg, two legs, all done. He yawned a big yawn. Mama read him a book about a little girl and her dog. Jaxson's eyes closed. The duck sat on the shelf and watched. "Night night, duck," Mama whispered.

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her swim suit all by herself. "Today I will swim," she said. Mum smiled and zipped the bag.

The pool was big and noisy. Leah saw the lifeguard sitting up high in a tall chair. "Why does she sit up there?" Leah wondered. Then Leah got in at the little steps. She held a red noodle. She kicked her feet. Splash, splash! The water was warm.

Then her hands let go. The red noodle floated away. Leah could not reach it. Before she could call out, a whistle blew. Tweet! The lifeguard slid down and reached with a long pole. The noodle came back to Leah's hands. "You saw me from up there!" Leah said. The lifeguard nodded and climbed back up. The room went quiet again. Leah held her noodle tight and kicked on and on.

Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia filled the little tub outside. Penelope splashed and splashed. Soon her arms were all wet. Drip, drip, drip went her fingers.

Tommy ran past her, dripping too. He ran to the sand box. Sand stuck all over his wet legs. "Oh no," said Tommy. "Sand on me!"

Penelope looked at the towel rack. She took a big blue towel. She rubbed her arms. Rub, rub. The towel made her arms dry and warm. Then she went to play, dry and happy.

Tommy came back. "Towel, please," he said. Teacher Mia smiled. "Kind Penelope can help you." Penelope patted Tommy's legs with the towel. The sand fell off, all clean.

"Now let's get dressed," said Teacher Mia. Penelope put on her dry socks. "Water day is the best day," said Tommy. Penelope laughed and wiggled her warm toes.

Rowan sat at the big kitchen table. The table was a rectangle. It had four corners. He touched each one.

Mama was baking cookies. The radio played a happy song. "Can I help?" Rowan asked. "You can cut the paper shapes," said Mama. She gave him safe paper scissors. Rowan cut a square. He started at a corner. Snip, snip. Then he cut a triangle. Start at a corner again.

Next came the circle. Rowan looked for a corner to start. He looked and looked. He turned the paper round and round. There was no corner at all. "Mama, my circle has no corner," he said. "A circle is round and has no corners," said Mama. Rowan laughed. He snipped all around the curvy edge.

A little milk almost spilled, but he caught it. His eyes stayed closed for one silly blink, then he looked. The circle was perfect. He held it up next to the round cookies. "Look," said Rowan. "Round like yours."

Sarah went to the store with Dad. Today was Monday. "Pancakes are on Saturday," said Dad. Sarah wanted pancakes now. "How many days is that?" she asked. Dad said, "Count with me." Sarah held up her little hand. They tapped each finger together. "Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday." Sarah looked at her fingers. Six days! Then she saw it. One more finger was still down. "A week has seven days," she said to herself, counting all her fingers. Seven felt like a lot of days.

Sarah and Dad walked down the store aisle. "Guess what we need," said Dad. Sarah pointed at the bread. "Yes! And look, these crackers are little triangles." Sarah picked up a triangle cracker box. "It looks like a little roof," she said. A lady walked by with a small dog in her arms. "What a cute dog," said Sarah. The dog wagged its tail.

At home, Sarah helped Dad put the bread away. She stood on her step stool, far from the hot stove. "Dad, is Saturday soon?" she asked. Dad said, "Sleep six times, and it is here." Sarah smiled. She held up her fingers and counted them again. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday. "I can wait," said Sarah. Dad kissed the top of her head. "Saturday pancakes for my girl," he said.

Ava sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture of her house. She took a red crayon and drew. Round windows, she made circles. She made a square door. She made a triangle roof. Her teacher, Miss Kim, put a wooden block on the table.

"Can you draw your house with this?" asked Miss Kim.

Ava looked at the block. She pressed it down on the paper. She traced around it. A square! She turned the block. She traced again. Another square. She turned it again and again. Six squares, all in a row. Then she had no paper left. "Oh no," said Ava. "My roof is lost! There is no room for a triangle."

Miss Kim smiled. "Count the sides of the block. Put a sticker on each one." Ava put a sticker on each flat side. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six square faces, just like that.

Ava stuck two squares together and folded them up. The squares made a little box, like a tiny room. She drew a circle window on it. Then she cut a rectangle door, careful and slow, while Miss Kim helped hold the paper.

Ava put her fingers on the box. It felt smooth, like the skin of an apple. She looked in the little door. A tiny paper cat sat inside. "The cat lives in the square house," said Ava. "Meow, meow!"

Arya went to the library with Dad. She wanted the book about the salty sea. "It lives on shelf five," said the librarian. Arya looked at her fingers. One, two, three, four, five. Then she saw the shelves. Each shelf had a number on top.

She found a shelf with a big 5. "Five!" she said. She counted her fingers again. One, two, three, four, five. The same five! The salty sea book sat right there. She pulled it out. "I found it!" she said. Dad laughed. "You clever counter."

On the way out, Arya counted the steps. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. The door let them out into the sun.

"Ten steps," said Arya. "Ten big steps!" Dad said, "Let's count them again on the way home." Arya held her book tight and began. One, two, three.

Willow's teacher put out a red mat. "Let's sort our toys," said Miss Kim. Willow sat down with her friends. There were toy cars, toy trucks and toy buses. They all had wheels. They were all the same kind of toy.

Willow picked up a car. Then she saw something yellow under the bus. It was a banana! Someone had put it in the toy pile. "The banana does not belong here," said Willow. "It is food, not a toy." Ben looked at it. "What do you call it?" he asked. "Miss Kim says it is the odd one out," said Willow. "It is the thing that does not fit in the group."

Then Willow walked to the snack table. She sat by the fruit bowl. Apples, pears and grapes sat there. A small sock sat there too! Willow laughed. She held up the sock. "Look! This sock is the odd one out now." She carried it to the dress-up corner and put it with the shoes.

Mohamed wanted his turtle book at bedtime. He ran to get it. "Read this one, Dad!"

Dad sat on the bed. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He read the little black marks on each page. His voice made the story grow bigger and bigger.

Mohamed pointed at a page. There was a big turtle on it. But the page had no little black marks. "Read this page too!"

Dad looked at it. He turned the page over. Then he turned it back. "There are no words here," said Dad. "Just the picture. There is nothing written to read."

No words? Mohamed leaned close. The turtle looked dizzy, spinning on his back. But the turtle said nothing. The page said nothing too.

Dad read the next page. Mohamed heard the words. The turtle found his feet again.

"More words," said Mohamed. He tapped the page. "Read them all, Dad."

Luca ran to the backyard. "Look, Mom! A big box tent!" Mom had made it from a cardboard box. Luca crawled inside. It was very dark in there. He wanted to wear his funny socks today. He dug in his sock bag. He pulled out two socks. "I got them!" he shouted. He ran to his bed and put the socks on his feet. Then he ran back out to the sunny grass. Luca looked down. He saw one red sock and one green sock! "Oh no!" he laughed. He looked at the yellow flowers and the blue sky. In the dark box, the socks had looked the same. In the bright sun, they looked so different! "Let me try again!" said Luca. He picked two socks in the dark tent. He ran out fast. This time he had two blue socks. "A match!" said Luca. Mom helped him clean up the box. Luca was happy. "Dark boxes are tricky!" he said, and he jumped on the green grass.

Wyatt wanted to play rocket ship. He found a big box in the hall. It smelled like cardboard and old tape. "I need a countdown," said Wyatt. But he did not know what a countdown was.

Dad was washing dishes. The water made a splashy sound. "What is a countdown?" Wyatt asked. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown," said Dad. He dried his hands and smiled. "Then you shout blast off!"

Wyatt climbed into the box. He counted one, two, three, all the way to ten. Then he counted backward. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Wyatt jumped up out of the box. He landed on the rug with a soft thump.

A small bug crawled near the box. Wyatt watched it go. Then he got back in. "Ten, nine, eight," he started again. Dad sat down on the floor to watch. "Blast off!" Wyatt shouted, and jumped higher than before.

Raphael was playing house at daycare. He put his teddy bear in a small chair. He gave the teddy a pretend drink from a tiny cup.

Then his friend Mia came over. She was holding her doll. Oh no! The doll fell on the floor. Mia began to cry. "Dolly fell down," she said.

Raphael picked up the doll. He looked at it. Was the doll hurt? He touched the doll's arm. It was soft, like a thick sock. The doll did not cry. The doll could not cry at all. Dolls are just toys. But wait, maybe it could feel better anyway?

Raphael gave the doll a big hug. "There, there," he said, like his mom said to him. Then he rocked the doll in his arms. Would the doll feel better now? He could not know. But he could pretend!

Mia stopped crying. She watched Raphael hug her doll. "Can I hug dolly too?" she asked. Raphael gave the doll back. Mia held it close and patted its little sock hat. "Dolly is all better," she said.

Raphael smiled. He went back to his teddy bear. He covered the teddy with a small blanket. "Night night, teddy," he said. The teddy lay very still. It was just pretending to sleep, just like the doll was just pretending to feel better. Raphael patted the teddy's soft head.

Mason wanted his brother's red kite. The kite was big. It had a long tail. Ben held it tight.

Mason reached for the kite. Ben pulled it back. "No, Mason. Ask me first."

Mason felt like crying. Mom knelt down by him. "You can say 'May I have a turn?'" she said. "It is a polite way to ask."

Mason tried. "May I have a turn?" he said.

Ben smiled. "Yes! You asked so nicely." He put the kite string in Mason's little hand.

Then a big wind came. The kite began to shake. The tail wiggled like a lion's tail. Mason held on tight. "Help!" he said.

Dad came fast. He held Mason's hand and the string too. "I have you," said Dad. The kite went up, up, up. It danced in the sky.

Mason watched it fly. "Thank you, Ben," he said.

"You're welcome," said Ben. "Now may I have my turn back?"

Mason gave him the string. Then he hugged his lion toy and sat with Mom on the soft grass. The red kite flew over their heads all afternoon.

Asher stood at the school gate. His backpack was on his back. It was very heavy. He could not walk fast. The straps pulled on his shoulders.

Mama said, "A backpack is a bag you carry on your back." Asher reached up and pulled the zipper open. He looked inside. He had packed three toy cars, a farm book, and a big rock from the yard. The rock was the heaviest thing of all.

He put the cars in Mama's bag. He put the rock in her bag too. He kept the farm book. Now his backpack was light. He walked through the gate all by himself. His steps felt bouncy and quick.

A boy stood by the door. His backpack slipped off, and his papers fell on the wet, slippery ground. Asher picked them up. He put them back inside the boy's bag. The boy smiled. Then he did something surprising. He took a small toy cow out of his pocket. "For the farm book," he said. "Can we read it together?" Asher grinned. He waved to Mama, and the two boys walked in.

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to draw a house for his brown teddy bear. But the roof would not look right. It kept coming out wobbly.

His friend Amna sat next to him. She had a sandwich. It was cut into triangles. Amna held one up. "One, two, three," she said. She touched the corners with her finger. "One, two, three," she said again. She touched the sides. Then she took a big bite.

Ibrahim leaned close. He counted too. "One, two, three corners," he said. "One, two, three sides." His teacher smiled and gave him a triangle stencil. "Try this," she said. Ibrahim drew around it with his crayon. The triangle sat on top of his square. Now he had a roof!

He drew a rectangle door. He drew a circle sun. Then he drew a brown spoon in a little bowl, because teddy bears get hungry. "Amna, look!" he called. Amna looked. "Nice roof," she said. Ibrahim hugged his paper all the way to the cubby.

Leah wanted to play hide-and-seek at the playground. Tom said, "I will hide first. You count to ten." Leah put her hands over her eyes. She said, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She said it very fast. Tom had not hidden yet. He was still standing by the slide. "Leah, you counted too fast!" he said. "Count slowly. Then we can hide."

Leah tried again. She covered her eyes. She counted, "One, two, three." Tom ran behind a tree. "Four, five, six." Tom ducked under the slide. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Leah opened her eyes. The playground was quiet. She looked behind the tree. She saw Tom's shoe! "I see you, Tom!" she called. Tom laughed and came out.

Then it was Leah's turn to hide. Tom covered his eyes and counted. Leah ran fast to the big line of bushes. She sat down in a happy little ball. Tom counted all the way to ten. Then he came looking. "Ready or not, here I come!" he said. Leah giggled behind the leaves.

Ryan sat at the little desk at the library. He wanted to write his name all by himself. A kind lady gave him a fat pencil and paper. "Grip it near the point," she said. Ryan held it tight and smiled.

He drew an R first. Then he drew a y, then an a, then an n. But he had started at the right side of the paper. There was no room left. His n squished into a tiny corner. Ryan made a sour face. "Too small!" he said.

He looked at the paper. Then he thought hard. He slid the pencil to the left side. He began again. R, then y, then a, then n. This time every letter fit. His whole name went across the page. Ryan lifted the pencil up high. "Look what I did!" he said. The kind lady clapped.

Sofia stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her red backpack with both hands. The hallway had a big window. Sofia looked out. The window showed the yellow school bus.

A boy on the bus stood up. He wanted to wave out the window. The bus driver looked at him. "Sit down, please," the driver said. The boy sat down in his seat. Then the bus began to move. Sofia watched. So that was it. On the bus, children stay sitting in their seats.

A girl named Mia walked up beside her. "What do you see?" Mia asked. "A bus," Sofia said. "The boy sat down. Then the bus could go." Mia smiled. "I have a sheep book," she said. "We can mix our books at story time."

The bell rang. The two girls walked down the hallway together. Sofia looked back once more. The bus was gone.

Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. The hairdresser, Miss Jo, put a cape on her. Snip, snip went the scissors. Beatrice watched the little hairs fall down.

"I want to see my hair," said Beatrice. She turned her head one way. She could see the front. She turned her head the other way. She still could not see the back. Her neck felt funny and itchy. She rubbed it with her hand.

"Wait right there," said Miss Jo. She picked up a small mirror. She held it up behind Beatrice's head. Now Beatrice could see the big mirror in front and the little mirror too. There was the back of her hair, short and neat.

"Oh! I see it!" said Beatrice. She stuck out her finger and touched the mirror. The girl in the mirror touched back. Beatrice giggled and giggled. "Hi, back hair!" she said.

Mila was going on a trip. Her family would sleep in a tent at a campsite. Mila put her teddy bear in her backpack. "He wants to see the tents too," she said.

First they went to the airport. It was big and loud. Mila held her backpack tight. A man at a long desk said, "Put the bag in the tray, please." Mila put the backpack in the grey tray.

Then the tray moved away. It went into a big machine. Mila could not see her teddy. "Where is he going?" she asked. "The machine checks what is inside the bags," said Dad. "It will look inside, and then your bag comes out the other end."

Mila watched and waited. She stood very still. Then the tray came out the other end. There was her backpack. There was her teddy! Mila hugged him tight. The lady at the desk smiled. "You were so patient," she said. Mila stood tall and proud.

At the campsite, the tent was red. Mila put her teddy inside. "Now you can see it too," she said. Outside, the trees went swish, swish. Mila yawned and closed her eyes.

Iris went to Papa's office with him. She saw a big tablet on his desk. "Can I draw?" she asked. Papa smiled and said, "Yes. First, tap the button on top." Iris tapped it. The screen lit up bright.

"Where is the drawing app?" she asked. Papa pointed. "See the small pictures? Those are called icons." Iris looked at them all. One icon had a little paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush icon. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" she said. She drew a green monkey with a long tail. Then she drew a sharp yellow star. She almost ripped the paper page under the tablet when she pulled it close. Papa helped her move it away.

When she was done, Iris pressed the button on top again. The screen went dark. "All put away," she said. Papa gave her a soft hug. "Good helper," he said.

Jules stood in the kitchen. He wanted to smell the bread. Mama put the warm loaf on the top of the counter.

Jules used his nose to sniff it. "Mmm," he said. "It smells good!" Then he had a question. How many holes does my nose have? He could not see his own nose.

Mama held up a little mirror. "Look," she said. "See your nostrils." Jules looked with his eyes. He counted one, two. "Two nostrils!" he said. "My nose has two openings!"

He sniffed the bread again. First one nostril, then the other. Both of them smelled the bread. What a fun surprise!

Jules touched the crust with his finger. It felt bumpy. He knocked on it gently, tap tap. It sounded hollow. "It talks!" he laughed.

Mama cut a slice. Jules took a small bite with his mouth. It tasted like yum. His ears heard the knock. His eyes saw the mirror. His nose smelled the bread. His tongue tasted it. His fingers touched it.

"It is late for lunch," said Mama. Jules ate his bread. "Knock, knock," he said, tapping his cup. "Who is there?" said Mama. "Bread!" said Jules.

Hudson stood in the school gym. He had a red beanbag in his hand. A hoop lay on the floor far away.

Hudson threw the beanbag overhand. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed with a soft sound on the mat.

"Can I try again?" Hudson asked.

"Yes," said Miss Kim. "Watch me. I will show you a new way."

Miss Kim held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop.

"Your arm starts low," said Miss Kim. "Swing it forward and up."

Hudson held his beanbag down low. He swung his arm forward and up. The beanbag sailed through the air. It landed near the hoop.

"Close!" said his friend Mila. "Try again."

Hudson tried again. Swing, up, drop. The beanbag fell right into the hoop.

"I did it!" said Hudson.

Then Miss Kim rolled a big blue ball to him. Hudson put out both hands. The ball bumped his chest and fell down. It was a messy try. He ran after the ball.

The ball came again. This time Hudson held both hands out wide. The ball landed in his arms. He hugged it tight.

"Nice catch," said Mila.

Hudson laughed and rolled the ball back. "Your turn," he said.

Matteo put on his new shoes. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. He held Mama's hand. One foot went up the step. Then the other foot went up too.

Inside was a big room. It was full of toys and kids. Matteo stood still by the door. He did not know anyone. A lady came over. She knelt down low.

"I am Miss Rosa," she said. "I am the teacher."

Mama nodded. "The teacher looks after the children," she said. "She helps them."

Matteo looked at Miss Rosa. She held out a red crayon. Matteo took it. He drew one sun. Then he drew another one.

"Hello, Miss Rosa," he said, very small.

"Hello, Matteo," she said.

Mama waved from the dark hallway. Matteo waved back with his crayon hand. Then he sat down to draw.

Billie ran to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on her face. She went to the little slide first. Then she saw the red truck at the far end.

"I want that truck," said Billie. She ran past the swings. She ran past the sandbox. She ran to the fence.

Billie looked back. She could not see Dad. The swings were in the way. She stood very still.

Then she heard Dad call, "Billie! Where are you?" His voice came from the swings. Billie ran back past the sandbox. She ran to the big tree by the swings. Dad was right there.

"There you are," said Dad. He held her hand. "Stay where I can see you."

They walked to the red truck together. The truck sat in the sun. Dad touched it first. "It is hot," he said. "We will find a shady truck."

They found a blue truck in the shade. It felt cool. Billie pushed it down the slide. It went fast. Dad clapped his hands.

On the way home they passed Billie's school. "My school," said Billie. "I sort blocks there. Red blocks go here. Blue blocks go there."

A lazy cat lay by the school door. It blinked one eye at Billie. Billie waved. The cat purred and went back to sleep.

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a heavy box under the toy shelf. He pulls it. He pulls again. The box does not move. It is too heavy.

Miss Ana brings him a light feather pillow instead. Carter picks it up with one hand. It is so light! He puts the pillow on the bottom. Then he adds one block, and another, and another. Slow, slow, slow he goes. The tower grows big.

The tower gets dirty on one side. Carter wipes it with a cloth. Then he puts the light pillow on top. It stays! Carter claps his hands. "My tower is big!" he says. Miss Ana smiles. "Can I knock it down slow?" asks his friend Milo. "No, knock it down fast!" says Carter.

Leah went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about animals. The books were all mixed up on the cart. "Which ones are animal books?" she wondered.

A boy named Sam was there too. He had a pile of picture cards. Sam put all the red cards in one pile. Then Leah had an idea. She took the red cards and made a new pile. She put the big red cards together. She put the small red cards together. "Look, Sam! Red cards, big and small!" Sam clapped his hands. Then he patted his toy lion on its soft nose. "Can we sort my lion too?" he asked.

The librarian smiled and brought three bins. Leah put toy books in one bin. She put food books in one bin. She put animal books in one bin. Then Leah found a funny book. It had a picture of an ugly green monster eating soup. Leah laughed. "Dad, look at this one!" Dad read it to her twice. On the way home, Leah held her new book tight and said, "Books can go in piles too."

Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house today. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not now," said Daddy. "We get there later. Now is this very moment. Later is after now." Paisley looked out the window. Now she saw a wild goose by a pond. Now the goose flapped and flew away. The goose was gone. It flew away and it did not come back.

"Yesterday we made eggs at Grandma's house," said Paisley. "Yes," said Daddy. "Yesterday is already done. Today we are in the car. Tomorrow we can make eggs again." Paisley clapped. Then she thought hard. She wanted to see Grandma. "Is it now?" she asked. Daddy laughed. "Not yet, sweet pea. First the road, then the bridge, then the hill. Then it will be now."

Paisley watched the road. The bridge came. Then the hill came. Then a red gate came. "Now?" she asked. "NOW!" said Daddy. Grandma stood by the red gate. She had a surprise in her hands. It was a little yellow hat, just Paisley's size. "I made it yesterday," said Grandma. Paisley put it on. "I learned to wait," she said. "Now I get hugs!" And she did.

Juliette was on the swim team. The team played in the big pool. The sun was hot. The tall coach blew her whistle. "Time for a break," she said.

Juliette looked for her water bottle. It was not there. She had left it at home. Juliette felt tired and hot. Her tummy felt wobbly.

The tall coach came over. She held a blue bottle. "Here, Juliette," she said. "Players drink water during breaks. Especially on hot days." Juliette took a big drink. The water was cool. Soon she felt better. Her wobbly tummy felt steady.
