Juliette went back in the pool. She kicked her legs. She splashed with her friends. The whistle blew again. "Break time," said the coach. Juliette ran to the tall coach. She took another drink from the blue bottle.

At the end, Dad came to pick her up. "Time to go home for dinner," he said. Juliette held Dad's hand. She would stay by his side all the way to the car.

"Next time I bring my own bottle," said Juliette. "Good idea," said Dad, and he smiled.

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name, Max. But the letters came out wobbly. The M looked like a squiggle. The A fell over sideways. Max made a sad face.

Grandma sat down next to him. "Hold the pencil near the tip," she said. She showed him how. Then she took a paper. The paper had dotted letters on it. "These dotted letters spell Max," she said. "You can trace over the dots."

Max pressed his pencil on the dots. He went dot to dot. Up, down, up, down. A wobbly M came out. He tried the next one. The A stood up tall. Max looked at it. "The dots help my hand!" he said.

He traced all four letters. Then he tried one with no dots. The M was almost straight. Max clapped his hands. His young brother clapped too, from his high chair. Grandma held the paper up so it would dry. Max laughed and said, "Now I write M-A-X!"

Florence ran to the shape table at school. There were squares, triangles, and rectangles everywhere. She wanted to find a circle to finish her picture.

Tommy held up his small button. "This can't be a circle," he said. "The clock is so big."

Florence looked up at the big clock. She looked at the tiny button. She put the button on her paper and rolled it round and round.

"Look, it goes round and round too," she said. "A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles!"

Tommy smiled and paid her a button from his pocket. Then he pointed at the window.

"A rectangle!" he shouted.

Florence tapped her cracker. "A square!" She tapped her napkin folded like a roof. "A triangle!"

Later, the class glued shapes into a paper nest with a round bird egg inside. The teacher said the nest was safe on the shelf.

Florence held up her button one more time.

"Tiny circle," she said. "Still a circle!"

Maria went to her music teacher's studio. Her teacher, Miss Ana, had a big drum there. "You can build a beat," said Miss Ana. Maria tapped the drum. Boom, boom! The sound was big like a lion. Maria tapped again. Boom, boom, boom!

Then Maria's mom and her friend Sam came in to listen. Maria played her drum song. Boom, boom, boom! The room felt hot from all the clapping hands. Everyone clapped and clapped. Maria just stood there. Miss Ana smiled and bowed down low. Maria watched her. Then Maria bowed down low too, just like that.

Everyone clapped again. "Yay, Maria!" said Sam. Maria drummed one more time. Boom! Then she bowed. "Again!" said Sam. Maria laughed and bowed again.

Ava sits at the art table. She wants to make a house. She takes a crayon and draws. The roof looks wrong. "My house is lost," she says. She means the shape is lost.

Miss Mia comes close. "Try this," she says. She gives Ava a small block. She gives her little stickers, too.

Ava puts a sticker on the block. One face. She turns the block. Another sticker. Two faces. She keeps turning. Three, four, five, six. Six stickers. Six faces. Each one is a square, like a window.

Ava smiles big. She dips the square face in paint. She presses it on her paper. A square print! She presses it again and again. Squares make a tall house wall.

Then she finds a paper circle. She presses it on top. It looks like a round sun.

"Look," says Ava. "My house came back."

Miss Mia peels the banana skin back for snack time. "Nice square walls," she says.

Ava takes her picture home that day.

Paint day was here at last. Charlotte ran to the art table. She wanted to paint a big rainbow for her mom. But there were only three paint pots. Red, yellow, and blue. Charlotte frowned. "Where are the other colours?" she asked. Her friend Tom, a boy with paint on his nose, said, "That is all we have today." Charlotte looked at her rainbow picture. It needed green and orange. She looked at the paint pots again. The teacher had left the pots open on the table. Charlotte dipped her brush in the blue pot. Then she dipped it in the yellow pot. The brush made a new colour on the paper. It was green! "Blue and yellow make green," Charlotte whispered. She tried red and yellow next. The brush made orange. Her rainbow grew and grew. Tom painted beside her, making purple with red and blue. Charlotte held up her rainbow. "Can I paint another one?" she asked. The teacher smiled and nodded. Outside, a dog barked at the sunny window. Charlotte picked up her clean brush.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her father put down a big pot of soup. "It's hot," he said. "I will pour it."

Zoey's little brother Sam sat in his high chair. He saw the soup and smiled. He was excited. He kicked his feet and laughed.

Then Sam grabbed his spoon. The spoon fell on the floor. He reached for it, but it was too far. His face turned sad. Then tears came. Big wet tears ran down his cheeks. When Sam felt sad, he cried.

Zoey looked around the table. She saw her bread. She held it out to Sam. "Do you want some?" she asked.

Sam stopped crying. He took the bread. He took a little bite. "Mmm," he said. Now he was happy again.

"Eat your soup too," said her father. "Careful, it's bumpy with big peas."

Zoey ate her soup. A pea rolled on her tongue. She chased it with her spoon. "Got it!" she said.

Sam laughed and clapped. "Zoey!" he said.

Lennon wanted to draw a big cloud. She could not find paper. Then she saw the library tablet on its stand.

Lennon tapped the top button. The screen lit up. On the screen were small pictures. One small picture looked like a paintbrush. Lennon tapped it. Tap! The drawing app opened, all by itself. She drew a fat white cloud. She drew a yellow sun too.

A boy came by. He looked sad. He wanted a turn. Lennon finished her cloud and showed him the paintbrush picture. "Tap this," she said. He tapped it and started to draw. Lennon pushed the button to make the screen dark. She put the tablet back on the stand, just where it belonged.

Henry went with Dad to the hospital. Mom had a new baby. The baby was so small and young.

The baby began to cry. "Why is he crying?" Henry asked. Mom said, "You can try to find out."

Henry looked at the baby. He waited. The baby kept crying. Henry saw the baby's mouth open and close. "Maybe he is hungry," Henry said. Mom gave the baby milk. The baby drank and stopped crying.

Later the baby cried again. Henry looked again. "Not milk this time," he said. He touched the baby's soft blanket. It had slid down. Henry pulled the blanket up. The baby stopped crying and went to sleep.

Henry gave the baby a kiss on his head. Henry's shoes still had sand from the park. He wiggled his toes and whispered, "Crying means you need me."

Hailey sat in the cafe with Mom. She had a pencil and a paper place mat. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

"Start with H," said Mom. Hailey pressed down hard. Snap! The pencil tip broke off. The little black piece rolled across the table. Hailey stared at the short pencil.

Mom gave her a new pencil. "Try again, sweet pea," she said. Hailey held it softly, like she was giving the paper a kiss. She made a light line. It stayed whole. She wrote H, then A, then I, then L, then E, and Y again. "HAILEY!" she said. Mom kissed the top of her head. "Pressing too hard on a pencil can break its tip," Mom whispered. Hailey made one more soft line. It did not break.

Lennon went to the library with her dad. She wanted to draw a big cloud. The paper box was empty. "All gone," said Dad. "Let's try the tablet."

Dad turned on the tablet. The screen lit up. Lennon saw small pictures on it. "What are those?" she asked. "Icons," said Dad. "Tap one and it opens an app." Lennon looked and looked. She saw a paintbrush icon. She tapped it. The drawing app opened! She drew a big white cloud. Then she drew a noisy goose under it. "I did it!" she said.

A boy came by. He wanted a turn too. Lennon tapped the top of the tablet. The screen went dark. She put it back on the shelf. "All done," she said. "Your turn." The boy smiled at her.

Hayden ran to the big library. He wanted a book about lions. But first he saw the playroom. It was a mess. Toys were all over the floor.

A girl was filling the toy box. "Blocks," she said. She dropped them in. "Blocks are toys." Hayden picked up a doll. "Dolls are toys," said the girl. He put it in the box. Then he found a ball. It had a loose thread on it. He pushed the ball in too. "Balls are toys," said the girl. Now the floor was empty. Hayden clapped.

The librarian gave him a lion book. In the book, a big elephant sprayed water. The elephant had a loose ear flap. It flapped like a wing. Hayden giggled. Then he closed the book very slowly. He wanted to see the elephant one more time. He opened it again. "Hello, elephant," he said.

Brielle got to school early. There was a new pencil on her table. It had a sharp point at one end.

"Today we write our names," said Miss Kim.

Brielle picked up her pencil. She ran to show her friend Milo. The point waved up in the air. Milo jumped back.

Miss Kim came over. "Hold the point facing down," she said. "Then it cannot poke anyone."

Brielle turned the pencil. The point looked at the floor. She walked back to her seat. Nobody got poked.

Brielle held the pencil with her little fingers. She wrote a big B. Then an R. Her hand went slow.

"Almost done," said Milo. He clapped.

Brielle wrote every letter. "That is my name," she said.

"Your turn tomorrow," said Miss Kim. "We can count the letters then."

Brielle smiled at her letters, all in a row.

Lily loved her school bag. It was big. Her friend Ben had a small bag. "One bag, two bags," they said.

At school, they played outside. Lily ran fast. Ben walked slow. The sun was hot. The water from the tap was cold. Lily washed her hands. A snail sat by the wall. "Slimy," said Lily. She touched it, very gently.

After lunch, the class had nap time. Lily closed her eyes. She slept and slept. Then she woke up. The room was dark. "It's morning!" Lily began to shout. "Time to play!"

Miss Maya came over. She opened the curtain a little. Lily looked out. The sky was black. One star, two stars, three stars. The sun was not there.

"It is still night," said Lily, quietly. "Night is dark. Day is light."

Miss Maya smiled. Lily went back to her mat. She closed her eyes. Outside, the stars stayed. One star, two stars, three.

Sara ran to the park with her little blue bunny. She set bunny on the bench. Then she ran to the slide. The slide was fast. The sand was warm. The swing went high.

"Now I want bunny!" said Sara. She ran back. Bunny was gone. Sara looked under the bench. She saw a cup. She saw a thin stick. No bunny. She looked by the tree. A dog began to bark. "Woof, woof!" Still no bunny.

A park helper came by. "Did you lose something?" she asked. "My bunny!" said Sara. "Come with me," said the helper. She led Sara to a small box. "This is the lost and found. People put things they find in here, so the owners can get them back." Sara peeked in. One mitten. Two hats. Three balls. And there, on top, sat bunny! "Bunny!" Sara hugged her tight. "The lost and found saved you!"

Sophie sat in the car. She sat in her deep blue seat. Mom sat in front with the new baby. The baby was wrapped in a soft blanket.

"I miss you, Mom," Sophie said. "Just you and me."

Mom looked back at Sophie. "I hear you," Mom said. "That is okay to feel."

Sophie counted the cars going by. One car. Two cars. Three cars. The baby began to cry. Mom sang to him. Then Mom sang to Sophie too. Sophie sang along. The baby stopped crying.

At home, Dad gave Sophie a cookie. Mom put the baby in his bed. Then Mom sat next to Sophie. Just Mom and Sophie, eating one cookie together.

"Again tomorrow?" Mom asked.

"Yes," said Sophie. "Cookie for two."

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum and two sticks. He wanted to play a song like the big kids.

On the stand there was a paper. It had dots and lines on it. "What are those?" Felix asked. Miss Kay smiled. "Let's find out," she said.

Miss Kay pointed at a dot. She hit the drum one time. Then she pointed at another dot. She hit it two times. Felix watched. The dots were telling her what to play!

Felix looked at the paper. He hit his drum one time, then two times. He waited. He looked again. He hit a slow beat, then a fast beat. "The dots talk to me!" he said.

A bird sat by the window. It sang along. Felix did not get upset when he missed a dot. He just looked again and tried once more. Miss Kay clapped. "Play it again," she said.

Felix hit the drum. The bird sang. The dots went up, and the sounds went up too.

Sofia wanted to play the senses game. Mama had promised it after supper. But Sofia could not remember them all.

"Let's start with eyes," said Mama. "Close them." Sofia closed her eyes. The room went dark. Then Mama turned on a lamp. Sofia opened her eyes. "I see light!" she said. "Eyes are for seeing."

Next came ears. A car went by outside, fast and loud. Sofia pointed to her ears. "Ears hear," she said. Mama smiled. Then Sofia smelled cookies baking. "My nose knows!" she laughed. Daddy gave her a cookie, cool and ready.

Then Mama put a soft sock on the table. "Which sense is this?" Sofia did not know. Mama took Sofia's hand. She pressed Sofia's fingertips on the sock. Soft! Then on a spoon. Cold! Then on the cat. Warm and furry! "My skin feels it," said Sofia. "My fingertips feel!"

"That's touching," said Mama. Sofia clapped. Five senses, all named. She touched Mama's cheek. "Warm," she said. "Soft too." Outside, the moon came up, and Sofia felt Mama's hand hold hers all the way to bed.

Mason lost his monkey. It was his favorite toy. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. He looked behind the big chair. No monkey.

Where could monkey be? Grandpa helped him look. They looked in the car. They looked by the swing. Grandpa said, "Maybe monkey went on the bus." Mason and Grandma walked to the bus stop. The bus driver held up a spotted monkey. "Is this yours?" she asked. Grandma read the tag. "It says Mason," she said. The driver smiled. "The name on the tag helped me know it was his."

Mason hugged his monkey tight. He said, "Monkey has my name!" He would build a little bed for monkey, right next to his own. "Good night, monkey," said Mason.

Ivy sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her teddy was missing from her bag. "Where did he go?" she asked. She looked with her eyes at the floor. She listened with her ears. She heard voices and a phone. No teddy.

The nurse smiled. "Maybe he fell in the exam room," she said. They walked in together. The room was dark. Ivy could not see much. "Too dark," she said. The nurse reached up and switched on the lamp. Click. Now the room was bright. Ivy saw her teddy under the chair. "There he is!" She ran and picked him up.

The doctor came in. "I hear you found your teddy," she said. "You have a good team." Ivy held teddy close. He smelled like soap. She kissed his soft ear. "You taste like breakfast," she said. The doctor laughed and laughed.

Adam was at school. It was counting time. Miss Kim sang, "One, two, three, four, five!" Adam clapped along. Then the song went on. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Adam liked the word ten. It felt big in his mouth.

After the song, Adam got paper and crayons. He wanted to write ten. He wrote a big 1. Then he stopped. "Why does ten need one more number?" he asked. Ben sat next to him. Ben showed his paper. Ten had a 1 and a 0, side by side. Adam looked hard. Then he made his own 0. He put it right after his 1. There it was. Ten!

Adam wanted to count real things. He found a fresh green leaf on the table. He counted it. "One," he said. He took a bite of his apple at snack time. Then he counted his crackers. One, two, three, four, five. Miss Kim gave him more. He counted on and on. Six, seven, eight, nine. "One more makes ten," said Adam. Ben laughed and clapped. Adam held up his paper. "Ten! A one and a zero!" he said.

Mateo was in the family car. "Where is Bunny?" he asked. Bunny was his favorite toy. Bunny was not in his lap. Bunny was not in his bag.

"I want Bunny!" said Mateo. Dad stopped the car. "Let's look," said Dad. Mateo peeked under the seat. It was dark under there. He saw no Bunny at all. He saw only a dark spot. "I can't see!" said Mateo.

Dad reached into the glove box. He took out a flashlight. He turned it on. He was the grown-up, so he held it. He shined the light under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore. Mateo could see everything! There was a cracker. There was some hair. And there, in the corner, was Bunny!

"Bunny!" Mateo shouted. He grabbed Bunny and hugged him tight. "The light helped us see!" he said. Dad laughed. "The shop by our house sells flashlights. We can buy one just for you."

"Yes, yes, yes!" said Mateo. He held Bunny up high. Bunny got a big kiss. Then Mateo sat back with Bunny. They were not alone anymore. The car drove on. The flashlight sat on the seat, still glowing bright. "Look, Bunny," whispered Mateo. "The light is still on!"

Matteo put on his new shoes. He tapped each foot, one, then the other. "First day of school," said Mama. Matteo held her hand very tight.

The classroom was big. It was full of toys and small chairs. Matteo did not know anyone. He hid behind Mama's coat. A lady with a red sweater came over. "Hello, Matteo," she said. "My name is Miss Jo. I am the teacher." She knelt down and smiled. She showed Matteo a box of blocks. She helped him stack one, then two, then three.

Mama sat on a little chair and waited. Matteo looked at her. Then he looked at Miss Jo. He took one small step. "Hello, Miss Jo," he said, very quiet. Miss Jo clapped her hands. Matteo stacked another block. It went up, up, up, and stayed.

Iris went to Mama's office. She saw a tablet on the big desk. "Can I draw?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "First we turn it on." Mama pressed the round button. The screen lit up. Iris tapped it too. The screen woke up again. The tap made it work.

Iris looked at the small pictures on the screen. One little picture had a paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" she said. Iris drew a green monkey with a long tail. She drew a banana too. Then she was done. She gave the tablet to Mama. Mama put it away in the soft bag. Iris looked at her paper cat next. She wanted to cut it out. "The scissors are sharp," said Mama. "I will cut it for you." Iris watched the paper snip, snip, snip. "Now it can stand up," said Iris.

Jordan planted carrot seeds at school. He made a deep hole with his finger. He dropped the seeds in the dirt. Then he patted the soil down soft.

Jordan gave the seeds water from a small green can. "Now grow, little seeds," he said.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He saw only dirt. No sprout. No green. He felt sad. His teacher, Miss Bea, sat with him in a circle on the grass. "Seeds need water," she said. "And they do not come up right away."

So Jordan watered the seeds again. He watered them the next day too. He shared his watering can with his friend Mia and her seeds.

One morning, Jordan saw something tiny and green. A little sprout! It was peeking up from the dirt. "Look, Mia!" he called. "My seed grew!" Jordan gave the sprout one more sip of water and smiled.

Grayson woke up and saw white outside. Snow! Lots and lots of snow.

"No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day."

Grayson wanted to play with his friend Nia. But first he had to find her. He could not call her. He put on his boots.

He stepped into the snow. His boots made marks. Each step made a print. He looked back and saw his own path.

Then he saw more prints. They were small prints. They went past the big tree. They went up the walk.

"Mom, come see!" said Grayson. "These are not my prints!"

They followed the prints. Step, step, step. The snow felt bumpy under his boots. The prints stopped at a door.

The door opened. It was Nia!

"I came to ask you to play," she said.

Grayson clapped his hands. "Your feet showed me the way!"

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. She held her fuzzy bear on her lap. "Open wide," said Dr. Kim. Grace opened her mouth. Dr. Kim looked at all her teeth. "Your teeth are clean," said Dr. Kim. "Do you know why? You brush them for a long time. Germs like to hide, but brushing finds them."

Grace wanted clean hands too. She went to the little sink. She pumped some soap. She scrubbed fast, fast, fast. Then she stopped. Was that long enough? She looked at her hands. "Hmm," she said. "How long is long?"

Then Grace began to sing. "Happy birthday to you." She scrubbed while she sang. When the song was done, her hands felt slippery and clean. She rinsed the soap away. The water ran cold, like ice.

"Now my hands are clean like my teeth," said Grace. She held up her hands for Dr. Kim to see.

"Yes they are," said Dr. Kim. "Do you want a sticker?"

Grace picked a shiny tooth sticker. She put it on her fuzzy bear. "Bear has clean hands too," she said.

Matteo wanted to win at hide-and-seek. He found a spot behind the short slide in the yard. The slide was like a little hill, and it was his hiding spot. Then he covered his eyes with his hands. Now nobody could see him. Or could they?

He heard his friend Pia laugh. He heard her shoes on the grass. "I see you, Matteo!" she called. Matteo peeked through his fingers. His eyes could see the slide, the fence and Pia's smiling face. When his eyes were closed, he could not see her. But her eyes were open. She could still see him!

After the game, Miss Dana gave out apple slices. Matteo smelled them first. Sweet! He touched one. It was cool and smooth. He took a bite. Crunch! "Do you like it?" asked Pia. "I do," said Matteo. He closed his eyes for one second. Still crunchy. Still yummy. Then he opened them wide again.

Gabriella sat on the small blue mat. Miss Polly, her music teacher, played a song on the piano. "Now we clap," said Miss Polly. Gabriella clapped. But her claps went too fast. Clap clap clap clap! Soon she was a whole big mess of claps. "I can't do it," said Gabriella.

Miss Polly stood up. "Let's march," she said. She marched around the room. Thump, thump, thump, thump. Gabriella marched too. Her feet went even, like footsteps when you march. Then Miss Polly said, "Now clap like your feet." Gabriella clapped. Clap, clap, clap, clap. Her claps matched her steps. They stayed even and kept going.

"Now let's sing," said Miss Polly. Gabriella sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" She clapped along the whole time. "You see," said Miss Polly, "steady as a sheep walking home." Gabriella smiled and clapped, clap, clap, clap, all the way to the end.

Kinsley sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump on the road. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "We will get there later."

Kinsley looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. The cow chewed grass. Yesterday Kinsley saw a cow too. That was yesterday. Today she saw a new cow. Tomorrow they would drive home again.

"Is it later yet?" asked Kinsley. Mom pointed to the clock in the car. "Look at the clock," she said. "The clock shows what time it is. When the little hand gets to the five, we will be there." Kinsley watched the clock. The little hand moved slow, slow, slow. It got to the four. Then it got near the five.

The car stopped. "Here we are," said Mom. "Now it is later!" Kinsley climbed down from her seat. Grandma held out a juicy red apple. "For you," said Grandma. Kinsley took a big bite. Then she found her book in her bag and sat on the porch step. The clock had said five, and now it was five. "We came at five," said Kinsley, turning a page.

Eliana sat in the car with her mama. They were going to the dentist. "My first time," said Eliana. Her tummy felt funny. Was she hungry? No. She had eaten breakfast.

The car stopped. They went in together. A big chair sat in the middle of the room. "Sit here," said the dentist. Eliana climbed up. Then a bright light glowed over her head. Eliana closed her eyes. It was too bright!

"Here," said the dentist. She gave Eliana little sunglasses. Eliana put them on. Now her eyes felt good. She opened her mouth wide. The light shone in. The dentist looked and looked. "I can see all your teeth," she said.

Eliana wondered. Did the light help the dentist see? She tried closing her mouth. The dentist could not see anymore. She opened it again. The light went in. The dentist smiled and counted every tooth. "Nice and clean," she said.

In the car, Eliana held her new toothbrush. "Mama," she said, "the light was so bright, but my sunglasses helped." She looked out the window. "Can the sun wear sunglasses too?"

Avery went to the store with Mama. The store had bright lights and big shelves. Avery saw a red apple. She wanted the red apple. She grabbed for it.

Mama shook her head. She held Avery's hand. Avery looked at the apple. Then she said, "Apple, please." Mama smiled and put the apple in the cart. Avery held the apple all the way to the bread aisle.

A little boy was there too. He reached for the bread. His mama shook her head. The little boy stopped. He said, "Bread, please." His mama gave him the bread. Avery watched. He got the bread, just like she got the apple.

At the checkout, they waited in line. First the lady in front went. Then it was Avery's turn. Avery put the apple on the belt. "Please," she said to the man at the register. The man smiled a big smile. He put the apple in the bag. Avery carried the bag to the car. "My apple," she said. "I asked so nice."

Henry went to the hospital with Dad. Mom was holding a new baby. "This is your baby sister," said Mom. She was very young and very small.

The baby began to cry. Henry put his truck down. The truck had sand in it from the yard at home. "Why is she crying?" Henry asked.

"She cannot talk yet," said Mom. "She cries to show she needs something."

"Maybe she needs milk," said Henry. Mom gave the baby some milk. The baby drank. Then she stopped crying. Henry clapped his hands.

The baby cried again. "Maybe she needs a hug," said Henry. Mom held her close. The crying stopped again.

Henry leaned over very slowly. He gave the baby a kiss on her head. The baby looked at him. "I will listen to you," said Henry. "Every day."

Gabriella sat on a small red chair at Miss Penny's music studio. Miss Penny put on a song. "Clap with me," she said. Gabriella clapped. But her claps went fast, fast, fast. Then they stopped. The song kept going without her.

Gabriella frowned. "My claps ran away," she said. Miss Penny smiled. "Try marching," she said. Gabriella stood up. She marched around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Her feet went even, like walking down the hall. The song kept going too. Her feet and the song went together.

"Can you clap like your feet?" asked Miss Penny. Gabriella clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Steady and even. Then she sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" She did not stop. She clapped and sang all the way to the end. Miss Penny clapped too. "Again!" said Gabriella.

Jordan planted seeds in the school garden. He made a deep little hole for each one. Then he patted the soil on top. "Grow, little seeds," he said.

Every morning Jordan ran to the garden. He saw a carrot patch. Maya's seeds had green shoots. Ben's seeds had green shoots. Jordan's pot had nothing at all. Just brown dirt. Jordan sat down in the circle of friends. He did not want to share his sad face.

Then he saw Maya hold her watering can. She tipped it over her shoots. Drip, drip, drip. Jordan touched his soil. It was dry and crumbly. He had never given his seeds any water. Jordan found his own little can. He filled it at the tap. He poured the water slowly and softly over the dirt.

The next morning, Jordan tiptoed to the pot. A tiny green shoot was peeking out. It had a little white hat of seed shell on top. Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little plant!" he called. Maya peeked over and smiled. "Mine did that too," she said. Jordan held up his watering can with both hands. "Water time," he said.

Ivy ran to the swings on a warm summer day. A little boy stood by the sandbox, counting his trucks. "One, two, four," he said. His face looked sad.

His big sister knelt down beside him. "You missed three," she said. "It goes one, two, three, four."

Ivy watched. The boy tried again. "One, two, three, four," he said. Now he smiled big. "More trucks!" said his sister. He counted on. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Ivy wanted to count too. She found ten little stones by the slide. She tapped each stone with one finger. "One, two, three," she said. She stopped. What came next? She thought hard. Then she heard the boy singing behind her. "One, two, three, four!"

"Four!" said Ivy. She tapped the next stone. Careful, she told herself, so the stones would not spill out of her hand. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten stones, all counted.

The boy ran over. "You said them all!" he said.

"Want to count my stones?" asked Ivy. She poured them into his hands. "One, two, three," they sang together, all the way to ten.

Jasmine ran to the door. "Park day!" she called. Her mom held up a bottle. "Wait, Jasmine. Sunscreen first." Jasmine stamped her foot. "Why?" she asked. "The sun is so shiny and bright," said Mom. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin." Mom rubbed it on Jasmine's arms. She rubbed it on Jasmine's neck. "Now we can go."

The park was hot and sunny. Jasmine played on the swings. The wind blew her hair. The wind blew the leaves. Big clouds came. Drip, drip, drop. Rain fell! Mom opened an umbrella. Then the rain turned soft and white. "Snow in summer?" asked Jasmine. "No," said Mom. "It is just petals from the tree."

Jasmine picked up a petal. She put it in her pocket to take home. Her friend Ben sat on the bench. His face was red. "I forgot my sunscreen," he said. Jasmine looked at her arms. They were not red. "Come on," she said. "My mom has more. She can rub some on you." Ben smiled and took her hand.

Hazel set her toys on the grass. She lined up her bear, her ball and her truck. Then she put out pretend food. There was a play apple, a play banana and a play cake. "Time to eat!" she said.

A soft sound came from the fence. Peck, peck, peck. A little brown bird was there. Hazel held out her hand very still. The bird flew down. It took a crumb of play cake and flew away.

Then Hazel saw something on the grass. It was small and gray and straight along one edge. "A feather!" she said. She ran to Mom. "A bird lost this. Birds are animals that have feathers." Mom nodded and smiled.

Hazel put the feather in her pocket. At bedtime it stayed under her pillow, straight and soft, waiting for morning.

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her little swimsuit. Her swim lesson started soon. "Why does the lifeguard sit up so high?" she asked Mama. "I wonder too," said Mama. "Let's go watch." They walked out to the pool. The lifeguard sat in a tall chair. Leah looked up, up, up. From up there, the lifeguard could see every swimmer in the pool. Then a boy splashed too far. He could not touch the bottom. His arm went up. The lifeguard blew the whistle. She jumped down fast. She helped the boy back to the wall. He held on and smiled. Leah's eyes went wide. "She was watching him the whole time," Leah whispered. After her lesson, Leah waved at the tall chair. The lifeguard waved back. "I saw you swim," she called down. Leah grinned all the way to the changing room.

Mason lost his monkey. His soft, spotted monkey was gone. He looked at Grandma's house. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the big chair. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey.

"Where can he be?" Mason asked. Grandma said, "Did you take him outside?" Mason had played by the gate. He ran to look. There was his monkey, sitting by the fence! But then a bus stopped. A kind driver held up the monkey. "Who lost this?" she asked. She looked at the tag. It said Mason. "This tag has your name," she said. "Now I know he is yours."

Grandma helped Mason write his name on the tag. Mason read it out loud. "M, A, S, O, N." His name was on his monkey. Grandma said, "Now everyone will know." Mason hugged his monkey tight. "Home with me," he whispered.

Athena went to the store with Grandma. Yesterday they had no milk at home. Today they needed to buy some. Athena held Grandma's hand in the big store.

Athena saw a pink balloon by the door. It floated up high. "Can I have one?" she asked. "Soon," said Grandma. "First we get the milk." Athena made a sad face. Soon felt like a long, long time.

They walked past the bread. They walked past the apples. Athena helped put the milk in the cart. Then they found cheese. The cart got full. It was not full yesterday. It was full now.

Then Grandma stopped walking. She pointed at the balloons. "Now," she said. Athena picked a pink one. She did not have to wait forever. Soon was just a little while.

At the bus stop, Athena held her balloon tight. The bus came down the street. "Today was a good day," said Grandma. Athena smiled. "Tomorrow can we come back?" she asked. Grandma laughed and hugged her. The bus doors opened with a big whoosh, and Athena stepped up, holding her pink string high.

Charles sat at book club. There was a big rug with letters on it. Miss Poppy pointed at the letters one by one. "A," said Charles. "B," said Mia. "P!" said Charles. He clapped. "I said them all!"

Miss Poppy smiled. "P," she said. "But P is not the end." Charles frowned. His sock felt itchy. He wiggled his foot. "Is P the last letter?" he asked. "No," said Mia. "Sing with me and see."

They sang the letter song. "Q, R, S," sang Charles. More letters came after P! He tapped each one on the rug. He got to the last square. "Z!" he shouted. "Z is the end!" He laughed. The song had hidden letters, like an animal hiding in grass.

"Now tell me," said Miss Poppy. "Where does it start?" Charles pointed. "A!" he said. "A starts it. Z ends it." Then he dried his hands on his shirt and sang the whole song again, all the way from A to Z.

Athena went to the store with Mama today. Yesterday Athena had seen pink balloons there. She wanted one so much. "Can we look now?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We will buy bread first. Later we will look at balloons."

Athena put the bread in the cart. She put apples in the cart too. "Is it later now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Soon, Athena. Soon means in a little while." Athena sighed. Waiting was hard.

Then Athena saw the bakery man put a cake in the window. His hands made the cake go round and round. The oven turned the cake big and gold. Athena watched. One thing made another thing happen. It was like magic, but real.

"Now it is later," said Mama. They walked to the balloon stand. Athena saw pink balloons, up high. "One for you," said Mama. Athena held the string. The balloon pulled her hand up, up, up.

"Tomorrow I will show it to Ben," said Athena. "Today it is mine." Outside, a big bus went by. The wind from the bus made her balloon dance. Athena laughed and held on tight. "Hello, balloon," she said. "We will go home now."

Wyatt wanted grapes. "You can have three," said Mom. Wyatt looked at the bowl. The grapes were small.

He picked one, two, three small grapes. Then he saw a big grape. It was fat and round. "Maybe a big grape counts as two," he thought. He put the big grape in his hand too.

Mom shook her head with a smile. "Three is three," she said. Wyatt put one small grape back. One, two, three. The big grape stayed. A little bug crawled on the table. Wyatt watched it while he ate.

The big grape was sweet and cold. Juice ran down his chin. Mom gave him a napkin. "One, two, three," Wyatt said again. He counted his grapes, and every time, three meant three. "More please," he said.

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. His big sister Poppy poured out buttons. "Let's count them!" said Oliver. "Yes!" said Poppy. She made two rows.

Oliver looked at the rows. One row went all the way across the table. The other row was bunched up in a small pile. "This one has more!" said Oliver. He pointed at the long row.

"Count them," said Poppy. Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the small pile. "One, two, three, four, five."

Oliver jumped up. "Both rows have five!" He pushed the long row close together. He counted again. Still five! He spread the pile out wide. Still five!

Oliver laughed. His soft toy bee sat by the salt. He made the bee hop over both rows. "Five and five!" said the bee, in a funny little voice.

Oliver counted one more time, just to be sure. "Five!"

Athena ran into the backyard. Her grandma sat on the step. The sun felt warm on Athena's arms.

"Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Athena nodded. She stayed close to the step.

Then Athena saw something. A little train went by, far away, behind the tall fence. It looked so neat! Athena ran to the far end of the yard. She stood on her toes. But the fence was too tall. She could not see the train anymore.

Athena turned around. The fence was big. She could not see Grandma. Her tummy felt small and tight.

"Grandma?" she called. There was no answer. Athena ran back fast. Grandma was on the step. She was waving. Athena ran right into her arms. That felt better.

"You came back," said Grandma. "You stayed where I could see you."

Athena sat next to Grandma. They heard the train together. Choo, choo! Athena counted the cars. One, two, three.

They counted to ten. The sun went soft and warm. Athena stayed on the step. Grandma held her hand. That was the best place to be.

Alexander dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped in a seed and patted it flat. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every morning he ran to the backyard swing. He swung high, then jumped off and looked at his garden. Nothing was there. Just dirt. Day after day, just dirt.

A bird landed nearby. It stuck out its tongue and chirped at the dry ground. Alexander touched the dirt. It was dry and crumbly, like crackers.

He ran inside. "Dad, my seeds will not grow!" he called.

Dad came out with the watering can. "Try this," he said. Alexander tipped it over the dirt. Water dripped down, dark and cool. He watered the spot every day after that.

One morning, something small and green stood in the dirt. It had two tiny leaves, new and soft. Alexander knelt down very close. "Hello," he whispered, and gave it a little more water.

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a house. He looked for a good shape. He found paper squares. He found paper circles too. Teacher Amna sat next to him. She had her brown spoon. She was mixing paint with it.

"Can a house be round?" Ibrahim asked. "No," he said. He put the circle aside. He picked up a square. He glued it down for the house walls. Then he looked for a roof. He held up a triangle. "How many corners does it have?" he asked. He touched each one. "One, two, three," he said. Three corners and three sides. The triangle sat on top of the square. The house had a roof.

Teacher Amna had her snack. Her sandwich was cut into triangles. Ibrahim pointed at a piece. "One, two, three," he said. Three corners again. She smiled and gave him a piece. He took a big bite.

Next to him, Sara dropped her brush. Paint was going to spill. "Teacher Amna!" Ibrahim yelled. She caught the cup with her brown spoon. Nothing spilled. Sara gave Ibrahim a paper rectangle. "For your door," she said. He glued it on. "One, two, three," he said, touching the roof corners one more time.

Harper sat in a big blue chair at the dentist. She held her gray mouse toy tight. "It will be okay, Mouse," she whispered. "One, two, three, we are brave."

A kind dentist walked in. His hands were blue. Harper stared. "Why are your hands blue?" she asked. "Do they hurt?"

The dentist smiled. "They are gloves," he said. He pinched one blue finger. Then he pulled it off. Under the glove, his hand was not blue at all.

"I wear the gloves when I put my fingers or my tools in your mouth," he said. "First I puts them on, then I looks inside."

Harper watched him snap on a new glove. The glove made a little pop sound. She giggled. "Say hi to my mouse first," she said. "He needs gloves too."

The dentist laughed softly. He held up one clean glove like a tiny blanket. He tucked it around the gray mouse. "All set," he said. "Open up, Harper. One, two, three."

Harper opened her mouth wide. Mouse watched from her lap, wearing his little blue blanket.

Henry put on his blue sweater. He ran to the park with Dad. The red truck was there. Henry wanted to ride it. But a girl was on it now. Henry had to wait. He felt a bit angry. He stomped his foot. Dad said, "We can come back tomorrow." Henry asked, "Where did today go?" Dad said, "After you sleep tonight, today will be called yesterday." Henry thought about that all day. At night he closed his eyes. He slept and slept. Then the sun came up. "It is today again!" said Henry. He ran to the park. The grass was wet. It had rained yesterday. The red truck sat all alone. Henry jumped on and rode round and round. "I waited, and now it is today!" he said. Dad clapped his hands.

Luna ran to the bookmobile. It was a little bus full of books. Dad held her hand.

"I want my own card," said Luna.

The librarian smiled. She made a card with Luna's name. "Pick one book," she said.

Luna picked a book about a red bird. She hugged it tight. "This book is mine forever!"

The librarian shook her head gently. "It has to come back on the due date," she said. "Then another kid can read it too."

Luna frowned. She did not want to move the book from her arms. The shelf looked empty where the red bird book had been.

"Will it be gone forever?" Luna asked.

"No," said Dad. "We bring it back. Then we can take it home again."

On the due day, Luna and Dad went back. Luna gave the librarian the book. She watched the librarian put it on the shelf. The empty spot was full again.

Luna picked it right up. "Hello, red bird," she said. "It's like a gift that comes back."

It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Grandma called, "Come help with the diyas!"

Eleanor ran to the table. The diyas were small clay cups. Each one was cool to touch. They had no fire yet.

Eleanor counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." She set them in a row. "Five, six, seven, eight." The row went all the way to the door.

"Are they ready?" Eleanor asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. He had the matches. He lit one little wick. A tiny flame popped up. Then another, and another.

Eleanor clapped her hands. "The dark went away!"

The diyas glowed orange and gold. The oil inside smelled warm and a little messy on her fingers.

"More, more!" said Eleanor.

Daddy lit the last one. Eight little lamps, all in a line.

"Now it is Diwali," said Grandma. "Look how our night shines."

Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table with her oatmeal. Her nose felt funny. Sniff, sniff, went Victoria.

"You need a tissue," said Mom. "Your nose is runny." Mom put a tissue in Victoria's hand. Victoria wiped her nose. The tissue was wet. She had not known her nose could do that.

Victoria went back to her oatmeal. Sniff, sniff. The runny nose came back. "Tissue, please," said Victoria. Mom smiled and gave her one. Victoria held it ready all by herself. She hoped her nose would feel better soon.

After breakfast, they looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. They saw the big tree in the yard. Victoria sniffed one more time. Then she picked up her tissue. "I can do it myself," she said, and she wiped her own little nose.

Axel sat down for dinner. He saw five carrots on his plate. "Wow!" said Axel.

Then he saw a big card by his plate. It had a 5 on it. "What is that?" he asked.

"That is the number five," said Dad.

Axel looked at the card. He looked at his carrots. He touched them one by one. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He held up his fingers too. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Dad laughed. "Yes! Five carrots and the 5 card. The same."

"I want to count more!" said Axel. He asked Dad for more corn. Dad put some on his plate.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight," said Axel. "Two more!"

Dad added two pieces. "Nine, ten!" said Axel. He clapped his hands.

Then Axel began to eat. He did not forget his carrots. "My tooth feels funny," he said. He pointed at a missing spot in his smile. "That tooth is missing!"

"Your big tooth will come," said Dad.

Axel grinned and took a big bite. "Ten bites!" he said. "One, two, three."

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. The room had small tables and many toys. A big bell sat by the door. When it was time to start, a teacher rang the bell, and the children came to sit down. There was a boy there named Sam. He had a toy car in his hand.

The teacher put out two bowls of crackers. She asked, "Which bowl has more?" Clara pointed at the tall pile in the red bowl. The teacher said, "Let's count and see." Clara touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three." The red bowl had more.

Clara wanted to eat a cracker. She took one from the red bowl. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four." Now Sam counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three." Clara said, "Mine still has more!" Sam laughed. He took one from the blue bowl too. Clara counted his bowl. "One, two."

Sam pushed his toy car across the table. "Now you have more than me," he said. Clara slid two crackers to his bowl. She counted both bowls. "Four and four. The same!" Sam clapped his hands.

The teacher rang the bell again. It was time for juice. Clara held Sam's hand, and they walked to the little cups together. "You can sit by me," said Clara. Sam rolled his car along beside her, all the way to the snack table.

Emile found a thick red book on the rug. The cover had a rabbit and a little flag. He wanted to know the rabbit's name. He opened the book at the back. He put his finger on the last page. He slid it from the right side to the left side. The pictures jumped around all wrong.

Miss Ana sat down next to him. "Let me show you," she said. She turned the book around. "This is the front." She opened the front cover. Then she put her finger at the left side of the page. She slid it from left to right. "Bunny hops," she said. The words came out in a row.

"Can I try?" Emile asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. Emile put his finger on the left. He slid it to the right. "Bunny hops to the flag," he said. He smiled and turned to the next page.

Bennett ran into the backyard. He wanted to splash in his little pool today. He saw Mama filling it with the hose. The water looked warm and nice.

"Can I jump in now?" Bennett asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. She put her hand in the water. "A grown-up has to check. The water must be warm, not hot."

Bennett waited. He touched the tall fence. He saw light on the grass. He did a little dance.

Mama smiled. "The water is warm now. You can get in."

Bennett stepped in slowly. The water felt good on his toes. He stayed close to Mama and splashed with both hands. Water flew up and up.

"Again!" he said. "Do it again!"

The bookmobile came to Luna's street. It was a little truck full of books. Luna held her mama's hand. The librarian smiled and said, "Today you get your very first library card." Luna took the card. It had her name on it.

Luna found a book about a red fire truck. She hugged it tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said. The librarian shook her head gently. "This book is borrowed," she said. "It has to come back by a certain day. That day is called the due date." Luna frowned. "Then it will be gone and the shelf will be empty."

"You can bring it back," said the librarian. "Then you can take a new one home." Luna thought about that. She moved the book in her arms and smiled. The librarian stamped a paper inside the book. Luna saw the mark. It showed the due date.

At home, Luna read the fire truck book three times. When the due day came, she and Mama walked to the bookmobile. Luna gave the book to the librarian. Then a boy took the fire truck book off the shelf. He hugged it, just like Luna had. Luna picked a book about the moon. "My new gift from the library," she said. The truck doors closed, and the bookmobile drove away. Luna waved until it turned the corner.

Bennett ran into the backyard. His dog Buddy was splashing in the little pool. Bennett wanted to jump in too. But the hose had been lying in the sun. Mom held the hose and let water drip on her hand. "Too hot now," she said. "Let it run and cool." Bennett waited on the grass. He patted Buddy's soft ears.

The water ran onto the ground. Bennett put his hand under it. First it felt hot like soup. Then it felt warm like a blanket. Mom put her hand in too. "Now it is just right," she said. Bennett stepped in slowly. The water made his toes feel happy. Buddy shook and water flew everywhere.

"Can we do this again tomorrow?" Bennett asked. Mom laughed and turned off the hose. Bennett waved to the tall fence, where the light of the sun made the water shine. Buddy barked once, and Bennett barked back.

Jules ran into the kitchen. Something smelled good. He used his nose to sniff. "Mama, what is that smell?" Mama was making pancakes. "Use your eyes to see," she said. Jules looked. Round pancakes sat on a plate.

Jules wanted to touch one. "Hot," said Mama. "You must wait." She put one pancake on a cool plate for him. Jules touched it with one finger. It was soft and warm. Mama poured batter into the pan. Jules heard it sizzle. Knock, knock. That was the door. "Daddy is home!" said Jules. He was not late after all.

Jules took a small bite. Yum, sweet! Then he wondered. How did his nose smell the pancakes? He ran to the hallway mirror. He looked at his face. There were two little openings in his nose. He breathed in. His nose moved a tiny bit. One opening, two openings. Both were working!

"How many openings does my nose have?" he asked Mama. He counted in the mirror. "One, two," he said. Mama laughed and put the top pancake on his plate. Jules sniffed it again. Both little openings took in the sweet smell. He took another big bite.

Snow fell past the window while Lucy played. "Look, a blue crayon," she said. Her brother Ben shook his head. "That one is too dark. That is not blue." Lucy held it up to her doll's dress. The dress was blue too, but a light blue, like the snow was almost white. "It is blue," said Lucy. "It is just dark blue."

"Let's ask the crayons," said Ben. They dumped them all out. Lucy picked the blue ones. "One, two, three, four, five!" She lined them up in a row. The first was very light. The last was very dark, deep as night. "They are all blue," said Lucy. "Light blue, dark blue, blue, blue, blue."

Ben tapped the darkest one. "Okay, it is blue. But it is sleepy blue." Lucy laughed. She drew a big deep blue sky. Then she added tiny white snow dots with her other hand.

Joshua ran into the school cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family! "I will stir the mix," he said. Teacher Mia smiled. Joshua counted the cups, one, two, three. He poured them in. He stirred and stirred. The mix looked like soft mud.

Next came the butter. Joshua opened the little fridge. He took out the butter. It was cold and hard. He pushed it with his spoon. The butter would not spread. It sat on the bread like a hard little rock. "Oh no," said Joshua. "My bread!"

Teacher Mia put the butter on the counter. "We will wait a bit," she said. Joshua waited. He tapped his spoon, one, two, three. Then he touched the butter. It felt soft now! He spread it on the warm bread. The butter went smooth and shiny. "Soft butter, happy bread, happy family!" Joshua carried the plate to the door. "Look what I made!"

Florence ran to the shape table at school. She wanted to make a sun for the class picture. The sun needed one big circle.

She found a big paper circle. Hooray! Then she wanted little circles for the sun's face. She found a tiny button on the craft tray.

Tom looked over. "That button can't be a circle," he said. "The clock on the wall is a circle. Your button is too small."

Florence held the button up high. She traced around it with her finger. Round and round it went. Then she looked at the clock. Round and round that went too.

"Watch this," she said. She pressed the button into the paint. She stamped it on her paper. A small circle appeared! She stamped it again and again.

"The big one is the sun," she said. "The little ones can be birds going to their nest." She stamped small circles across the sky.

Tom grabbed a button too. "I want to pay for my picture," he said, and he glued a button on like a coin. "A circle for money!"

Miss Patel hung both pictures on the safe wall by the window. Florence pointed at her sun. "Big circle, lots of little circles," she said. "They all go round!"

Bennett was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home soon. Bennett wanted to give her a gift.

"Let's make a picture," said Grandma. Bennett got his pencil. He drew a baby. He drew a cat. He drew a big red heart. Then he used the scissors to cut the paper. Grandma held the paper while he cut. The picture came out just right.

Next they went to the baby store. There were tiny socks and tiny hats. A boy there asked his mom, "Why so many diapers?" His mom said, "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet." Bennett listened. His baby sister would need lots of diapers. He counted them on the shelf. One, two, three, four, five. He put a big pack in the cart.

At last the baby came home. Bennett felt a little sad he could not play with her yet. But she grabbed his finger. Then she grabbed his picture too. Grandma put a fresh diaper on her. "Diaper, picture, baby," said Bennett. "All done." The baby yawned and fell asleep in Grandma's arms.

Madeline went to the park with her dad. She wanted to paint a pink flower for Grandma's card. She had red, yellow, blue and green paint. But no pink paint at all.

First she looked around the park. She saw green grass. She saw a blue swing. She saw a yellow slide. She saw red flowers by the bench. "Red flowers are pretty," said Madeline. "But Grandma loves pink."

She sat at the picnic table. She opened her red paint. She dipped her brush. She painted a red flower on the card. "Too red," said Madeline. She wanted pink, pink, pink.

Then she saw a big bucket of white paint. Dad was painting the fence with it. Madeline had an idea. "Can I have a little white, please?" she asked. Dad helped her put one drop of white in her red paint. Madeline stirred it round and round, slowly, slowly. The red paint turned pink! "It's pink!" said Madeline. "White made my red light!"

She painted a pink flower for Grandma. She painted one pink petal, two pink petals, three pink petals. Then she ran to the high slide and slid down fast. Dad said, "Grandma will love it." Madeline held up her card and smiled. "Pink flower for Grandma!"

Anna was playing in the yard. The wind began to blow. Sand flew up in the air. Some sand got in Anna's eye. She blinked and blinked. "Ow," she said. The sand went away. Anna ran to Mama. "Why do my eyes blink at sand?" she asked. "Try and see," said Mama. Anna blinked again. She made it fast, then slow. Her little hairs on her eyelids moved too. "The sand lands on them," Anna said. "Then it falls off!" She put her hand near her eye. The soft little hairs tickled her finger. Anna heard the wind again. She smelled the flowers by the door. She touched the warm wall. The wind blew more sand. Anna blinked fast. Not one bit went in. "My eyelashes keep dust out of my eyes!" Anna said. She made a robot face. "Beep beep. My robot eyes are safe." Mama laughed. "Will the sand make you sad now?" she asked. "No," said Anna. "I cannot lose. I have eyelashes!" She ran back to play.

Parker stood at the edge of the pool. The water was bright green and warm. His mom held his hand.

"Look up high," said Mom. Parker looked. A lady sat in a tall chair above the water. She wore a red suit and big sunglasses.

"Why is she up there?" Parker asked.

"She is the lifeguard," said Mom. "Her job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it."

Parker kicked his feet in the water. He held the wall. He let go for one second. Then he slipped. His arms went splash, splash.

The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed right at Parker. A pool helper came over fast and held him up.

"I saw you from up high," the lifeguard called down. "I can see everyone up here."

Parker looked up at her tall chair. From there she could see his mom, and the kids, and the whole pool.

Then it was time for lunch. Parker sat on a towel and ate cheese and crackers. After lunch, a green ball floated by. Parker tried to chase it along the edge. The lifeguard watched him the whole way.

"Nice walking, Parker," she said from up high. "I am still watching."

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to play a song, but he did not know how.

Miss Kim had a big paper on the stand. Felix saw dots and lines on it. "What are the dots?" he asked.

Miss Kim smiled. "Those are notes," she said. "The notes show which sounds to play." She pointed. "Play here. Then here. Then here."

Felix hit the drum at each note. Boom. Boom. Boom. He waited between the notes. He tried again, slow and slow. The booms made a song!

A bird sat at the window. It cocked its head. Felix did not feel upset anymore. He played the song one more time, boom by boom. The bird stayed to listen.

Juliette loved her soccer team. They played by the big pool. The grass was green and soft.

"Kick the ball to the goal," said Coach Ben. He pointed to the net far away. Juliette ran to the ball. She kicked it hard. But the ball went the wrong way! It rolled toward the tall net behind her.

"Oh no," said Juliette. The ball bumped into the net. The other team did not get a point. Coach Ben ran over. He turned Juliette around with kind hands. "Look this way," he said. "See that net? Kick there."

Juliette looked. The net was far away, by the pool fence. She got the ball again. She looked at the net first. Then she kicked. The ball rolled and rolled. It went into the net! "Goal!" her friends cheered.

Juliette clapped her hands. She kicked the ball the right way now. After the game, they would all stay for dinner by the pool. "I can kick to the net," Juliette told Coach Ben. He smiled and gave her a big thumbs up.

Henry went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so he could not go. "When can we play?" Henry asked. "Now," said Mom. Henry ran to the swings.

"Now we swing," said Henry. "Later we will get ice cream." But when was later? Henry asked again and again. Mom held up her phone. On it was a clock. "This clock shows what time it is," she said. The little hand pointed to a three. "When the hand moves to four, we go." Henry watched the hand. It did not move. He waited. He swung high. Then he looked again. The hand had moved! "It is four!" he shouted.

They got ice cream. Henry was not angry about waiting anymore. "Tomorrow," he asked, "can the clock say park time?" Mom laughed. "Yes. And tonight it will say bedtime." Henry licked his cone and waved goodbye to the swings.

Margot sat on her bedroom floor. She wanted to write a note. It would say, "Come read to me, Grandpa." She held her crayon tight. She wrote and wrote. Then she ran to find Grandpa.

"Read my note!" said Margot. Grandpa looked and looked. He turned his head sideways. "Hmm," he said. "It says gobbledygook. Is it about a stinky sock?" Margot giggled. "No! It is not stinky! It says come read to me!" Grandpa shook his head. "All your letters are holding hands. One, two, three, four, all squished in a big hug."

So Margot went back to her note. She counted her words. One word: come. Two words: read. Three words: to. Four words: me. She left a little space after each word. "Words need a space between them," said Grandpa, peeking in. Margot added the spaces, one by one.

"Try now!" she said. Grandpa read it. "Come read to me, Grandpa!" he said out loud. "Why, yes! I will!" They sat on the bed. Grandpa opened the book at the front. He read page one. Then page two. Then page three. Margot snuggled close and said, "Now we sink into the pillows, too."

Parker stood by the big blue pool. He wanted to swim like the big kids. Mom held his hand. "You can learn today," she said.

Parker looked up at the tall chair. A lifeguard sat up high. "Why does she sit way up there?" Parker asked. Mom said, "Watch and see."

Parker got in the shallow water. It was cool on his toes. He kicked and kicked. Then he saw a green ball float far away. He tried to chase it. His feet slipped. He went under for a moment.

Splash! The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed right at Parker. A helper came fast and lifted him up. "I saw you from up high," the lifeguard said. Parker held the helper's hand. From the tall chair, she could see everyone in the pool.

Parker kicked back to the steps. Mom hugged him. "Swim time is done for now," she said. "Lunch soon."

Parker looked up at the tall chair. He waved at the lifeguard. She waved back and kept watching the water.

Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked for orange paint. There was no orange paint at all.

"What can I do?" Norah asked her teacher. Her teacher smiled. "Ask Milo. He knows a trick."

Milo came over with two pots. He dipped his brush in red paint. Then he dipped it in yellow paint. He stirred them together on his paper. Swish, swish, swish. The paint turned orange! It smelled a little stinky, like all the paints did.

Norah dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred. Orange! She painted her pumpkin round and bright.

"I did it," said Norah. "Red and yellow make orange."

Milo laughed. "Now pay me back with a big smile."

Norah smiled her biggest smile. Then she painted a green leaf on top.

Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. It was her first haircut. The hairdresser, Mia, snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down like snow.

Beatrice looked in the wall mirror. She could see the front of her hair. It was short now. "I want to see the back," said Beatrice. She turned her head. She could not see the back. She stuck out her chin. She turned again. Still no back. "I can't see it," she said. "That is not bad," said Mia. "I have an idea."

Mia held up a little mirror in her hand. She held it behind Beatrice. Beatrice looked at the wall mirror. There it was! The back of her hair. She could see it in the small mirror. "I see it! I see the back!" said Beatrice. She wiggled her toes. "Do it again," she said. Mia smiled and held the little mirror up once more.

Brooklyn got her red coat from her room. But the coat was not on the hook. It was on the floor, under her toy carrot! "Where is my coat?" she asked. She looked and looked. There it was, down low, all crumpled up.

Mama hung the coat on the hook. "Now it waits up high," said Mama. Brooklyn put her arms in the sleeves. One arm, two arms. Then she pulled the zipper. Up, up, up it went. Zzzz! The coat was warm and furry like a cat.

At the bus stop, Brooklyn waited. The bus was not here yet. So she dreamed about the carrot in her pocket. The bus came. She climbed up. "I zipped it all by myself," she said. Mama smiled and zipped her own coat too.

Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table for breakfast. The sky outside was cloudy. "Sniff, sniff," went Victoria's nose.

Mama gave her warm oatmeal. Victoria took a bite. "Sniff, sniff," went her nose again. She wiped it on her sleeve. Her sleeve got wet and sticky. That did not feel good.

"Let's name what your nose needs," said Mama. "A napkin? No. A towel? No. A tissue? Yes!" Victoria took a tissue from the box. She blew her nose, one big toot. Now her nose was clear.

After breakfast, Victoria sat by the window. She could smell her apple now. She watched the big tree sway. "I hope we can play under it soon," she said. She held the tissue box on her lap, all ready.

Elijah put on his skates at the ice rink. The ice looked fresh and shiny. His dad helped him step onto it. His mom held one hand. His friend Nina held the other.

They skated slow. They skated past the snack bar. On a big screen, a basketball game was playing. A man blew a whistle. All the players stopped running. Elijah stood still on his skates. "Why did they stop?" he asked.

Nina pointed at the screen. "The whistle," she said. The whistle blew again. The players started running again. Elijah watched with wide eyes. The whistle blew. The players stopped. The whistle blew. The players ran.

Then the game ended on the screen. Dad bought warm cocoa for everyone. Elijah took a little sip. Mom gave his hair a kiss. They sat and watched the skaters go round and round. Elijah listened for more whistles. "Listen," he said. "That horn means the zamboni is coming."

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She had blocks of many shapes. She found a round block. It rolled away. "Too wobbly!" she said. That block was a circle, and circles roll.

She found a block with three sides. "A triangle!" It made a fine roof, pointy at the top. Then she found a long block with four sides. A rectangle! Perfect for the wall.

She looked for one more square block. Her friend Ben pointed at a tilted block. "Look, a new shape!" he said. "It has a corner pointing up!"

Lillian turned the block back down flat. It was the same square! She laughed. "Silly block. You are still a square!"

She stacked the square at the bottom. The house stood tall. She tucked the snake inside. "Home at last!" said Lillian.

Violet got to daycare in the morning. The sun was low and yellow. She put her coat on her hook. She wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. But paint time was later, after snack.

Violet played with blocks. She poured cold water in the sand table. The sand turned dark and sticky. "Look," said her friend Sam. "The water made it wet."

Violet ate her snack. Then the class went outside. The sun was high now. It was hot on her shoulders. After outside time came lunch. After lunch came a nap.

Violet slept on her little mat. When she woke up, she rubbed her eyes. "Is it morning now?" she asked. "Can I paint now?"

Teacher Mia shook her head and smiled. "It is afternoon now, Violet. The morning went by. It is nap-then-play time."

So it was afternoon. The sun was on the other side of the window. Violet sat at the paint table. She painted a big yellow sun.

"That is for Grandma," she said. Grandma would come this afternoon, after daycare. Tomorrow Violet would paint her a moon.

Emile wanted to find the dog in the book. He opened the book from the left. The pages went the wrong way. They would not turn.

His friend Noa came over. She held up a small flag with blue stripes. "This book is Hebrew," she said. "It opens from the other side."

Emile looked at the back of the book. He tried it. The cover opened! The thick pages turned one by one.

Noa pointed to the little letters. "We start here," she said. She pointed to the right side of the page. Emile put his finger there too.

They slid their fingers to the left. The letters made words. The words made the story. And there, on the last page, was a big brown dog.

"Woof!" said Emile.

Lily loved school. She loved the big blocks and the small cups. She loved the fast slide and the slow snail. The snail left a slimy line on the wall. Lily named her snaily things all morning. "One, the slide. Two, the snail. Three, the blocks."

At nap time, Lily lay on her mat. The teacher turned off the sun lamp. The room went dark. Lily closed her eyes. Then she woke up. The window was black. The stars were out. "It's morning!" Lily began to shout. "I want my snack!"

The teacher came over. She knelt down by the mat. "Look out the window," she said. "It is dark. It is still night. Day and night are opposites." Lily looked. Dark sky, little stars. Not morning at all. Day was bright, and night was dark.

Lily lay back down. The teacher covered her with a soft blanket. The blanket was warm. Lily's water cup was cold. She took one small sip. "One, sip. Two, blanket. Three, sleep," Lily whispered. Then the teacher wrote a letter to Lily's mom. It said Lily slept all night long. Outside, one star blinked, and Lily's eyes blinked too.

Raphael was playing house at daycare. He stirred a big pretend soup. His friend Mia held her doll, Baby Nell.

Then Mia dropped Baby Nell on the floor. "Oh no!" she cried. "Baby Nell is hurt!"

The teacher knelt down. "Look," she said softly. "The doll is not hurt. Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Mia wiped her eyes. She picked up Baby Nell. She gave the doll a big pretend hug. "There, there," she said. Baby Nell still looked the same. But now Mia smiled.

Raphael watched. Was that how it worked? He looked at his teddy bear. He squeezed the teddy's paw. The teddy did not say ouch. The teddy was just soft and quiet.

So Raphael tried it too. He held his teddy close. "You lost your sock," he told the teddy. He pulled a thick, cozy sock from the dress-up basket. He put it on the teddy's foot. "Warm now?" he asked.

Mia came over with Baby Nell. "Our babies can play," she said. Raphael gave the teddy another hug. "I thank you for the soup," he said in a small teddy voice.

The teacher brought real juice cups for the children. Raphael drank his juice. The teddy just sat there. That was okay. Pretend hugs were still nice.

Raphael patted the teddy's head. "Nap time," he whispered.

Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet book. She wanted to know every letter. Mom sat next to her on the soft cushion.

"Let's count them," said Mom. Brielle pointed at each letter. "A, B, C, D." She went on and on. Her sock slipped off one foot, but she kept pointing. "W, X, Y, Z."

"I counted all the way to twenty-six!" said Brielle. Her eyes got big. She counted again to be sure. Twenty-six again!

Then she made the letter sounds. "B says buh. B is for book!" She hugged the book.

"Now let's clean up," said Mom. Brielle put on her sock. She picked up her toys. "A is for away," she said, pushing the truck away from the nook. "A says ah!"

Mom laughed. "You did it, Brielle."

Brielle smiled and traced the letters with her finger, all twenty-six.

Mila wanted to play tea party in her playroom. She set out one big cup and one small cup. The big cup was for Teddy. The small cup was for her. "Pretend tea is not hot," said Mama. "It is cold, like water from the fridge." Mila touched it. "Cold!" she said.

Then Mila found a puddle by the toy shelf. It was small at first. She stepped in it. Splash! Now the puddle was big. Now her socks were wet. "My socks are wet," said Mila. "They were dry before. Wet and dry are opposites, Mama?" Mama smiled. "Yes, wet and dry are opposites." So they got dry socks.

Mila put them on slowly, wiggling her toes. Then she ran fast to the tea table. "Slow toes, fast toes!" she said. Teddy's tail was warm and soft in the sun. Mila hugged him and poured more cold pretend tea.

Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia filled the big tub. Penelope put her hands in. Splash! The water jumped up. Now her arms were wet.

Splash went Tom next to her. Now his shirt was wet too. Then the water play was over. Tom ran to the blocks. Drip, drip, drip. Water fell on the floor. "Wet boy, wet boy!" laughed Penelope. Tom looked down at his shirt. He was all drippy.

Teacher Mia held up a big soft towel. "Come here, Tom," she said. Tom came back. Mia rubbed the towel on his arms. Rub, rub, rub. The towel drank up all the water. Tom was dry! "My turn," said Penelope. Mia dried her hands too. Then Penelope got the towel and dried her friend Sam, one kind pat at a time. "All dry!" said Penelope. "Now we color." Sam handed her the crayon.

Alexander dug three little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed into each one. Then he patted the dirt down with his hands. "Now grow," he said.

Dad filled a small watering can. Alexander tipped it over the dirt. The water made dark wet spots on the soil. "Seeds need water to start growing," said Dad.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout. His dog, Biscuit, wagged his tongue and sniffed the ground. "Nothing yet," said Alexander.

He watered the dirt again. He swung the can back and forth. The sun felt warm. A ladybug landed on his new red boot.

The next day, more water. Still just dirt. Alexander waited on the swing and counted clouds.

On the fourth morning, Alexander ran to the garden. Something green was poking up. "A sprout!" he shouted. He knelt down very close. The tiny sprout had two little leaves. Biscuit barked once. Alexander ran to get his watering can.

Mason wanted to hold the red balloon. It was Daddy's balloon from the party.

Mason grabbed for it. The string slipped away. Daddy shook his head. "Try again," Daddy said.

Mason thought hard. He remembered his lion book. The little lion wanted a turn with the ball. The little lion said, "May I have a turn?" Then he got the ball.

Mason took a big breath. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Daddy smiled wide. "Yes, you may!" Daddy put the string in Mason's hand.

The balloon bumped the ceiling. Mason laughed and laughed. He held the string with both hands. The balloon went up, then down, then up again.

"Thank you, Daddy," Mason said. Daddy gave him a hug. "You asked so nicely," Daddy said. "That was very polite."

Mason walked slowly with the balloon. The lion book sat on the shelf. "Night night, lion," Mason whispered. The balloon floated above his head.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a pencil by his hand. "You can write your name," she said. Jackson picked up the pencil. He held it up high and waved it. Mom took his hand gently. "Point it down," she said. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone." Jackson turned the pencil. The point went down toward the table.

He pressed the pencil to the paper. He made a big round shape. "That is J!" said Mom. Jackson clapped. He tried again. He made an a, then a c. One letter went crooked. It slid off the paper. "I miss one," said Jackson.

"That is okay," said Mom. "Try again." Jackson held the pencil tight. He wrote k, then s, then o, then n. "Jackson!" he shouted. Then the pencil rolled. It stopped by the wet spot near his cup. Jackson picked it up, point down. Mom smiled. "Look at my name!" said Jackson.

Eliana sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Where are we going?" she asked. "To the dentist," said Mom. "She will look at your teeth."

At the dentist's office, there was a big chair. It went up and up when the dentist pushed a button. Eliana sat in the chair. She opened her mouth wide. Then a bright light above the chair turned on. Eliana squinted. "Too bright!" she said.

The dentist handed her little sunglasses. "Here, try these," she said. Eliana put them on. Now the light did not hurt her eyes. She could see the light shining right at her mouth. "The light helps me see inside your mouth," said the dentist. She looked at every tooth. "Your teeth are clean and strong," she said.

On the way home, Eliana was hungry. Mom gave her a snack in the car. Eliana chewed slowly. "My teeth taste the apple," she said. "Just like the light saw my teeth?" Mom laughed and drove on. "Can we come back?" Eliana asked. "Next time I want the sunglasses again."

Mohamed wanted a bedtime story. He ran to the shelf and grabbed his book. But it was Dad's old book, the one with funny letters.

Mohamed opened it from the left side. He saw pages with no pictures. He turned one page. Then another. Where were the pictures? He felt dizzy from all the little marks.

"Maybe I opened it the wrong way," he said. He closed the book. Then he opened it from the other side. The first page had a big sun! Under the sun were little marks too.

Dad sat down beside him. "Read with me," said Dad. Dad put his finger at the right side of the page. His finger moved to the left. The marks made words, and the words made the story of a turtle who wanted to grow big.

"Again," said Mohamed. Dad turned the page. His finger started at the right again. Mohamed put his little finger next to Dad's big finger. "My turn," he said.

Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. He found only three pots. "Red," said Leon. "Yellow. Blue." Three pots. Only three. Leon felt sorry for his rainbow.

Then Leon had a big want. He wanted orange for his rainbow. He dipped his brush in red. He tapped it on the paper. He dipped his brush in yellow. He tapped it next to the red. The red and the yellow sank together. The paint turned orange! Leon clapped his hands.

"Orange, orange, orange!" he sang. He painted a big orange stripe. He dipped in yellow. He dipped in blue. Tap, tap. The paint turned green! A green stripe went on the paper.

Red, yellow, blue. Three little pots. Blue and red made purple next. Leon looked at his rainbow. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. "I made it," said Leon. He held his painting up to the blue, blue sky.

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a small red block first. It is light. He picks it up easy. Then he finds a big basket of blocks. He pulls and pulls. It will not move. It is heavy. His friend Mia comes over. She pats the basket. "Heavy and light are opposites," she says. They take the blocks out one by one. Each block is light. Carter stacks a big block at the bottom. He stacks a small block on the top. The tower grows tall. Mia brings a pillow, soft and light as a feather. She sets it on the top. The tower wiggles. It wiggles slow, then it falls fast. The pillow lands with a soft plop. Carter laughs. He stacks it again, slow and careful. "Look at the top," he says. The pillow sits there, all warm in the sun, while the cold juice cups wait on the shelf.

Mila wanted to find her red sock. It was lost somewhere in the playroom. She looked under the big teddy bear. Not there. She looked in the small toy box. Not there.

Then she saw her dog, Max, by the door. His tail was wagging fast. "Do you know where my sock is?" she asked. Max wagged his tail slow and happy. He was sitting on something. It was the red sock! But the sock was wet. Max had dripped water on it from his walk. "Wet sock," said Mila with a sigh. "I need a dry one."

Mila put the wet sock on the warm radiator. Mom helped her stay far from it, because it was hot. Then Mila found a dry blue sock in her drawer. She put it on her small foot. Max licked her toe, fast then slow. "Good boy," said Mila. "Now my foot is dry, and my sock is not!" She patted his soft ear, and they sat together on the rug.

Milan went to the park with his dad. He saw a red strawberry in the picnic basket. "Can I have it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. Milan loved strawberries.

First, Milan smelled the strawberry with his nose. It smelled sweet. Then he took a bite. It tasted big and sweet. Then he had a funny idea. What if he held his nose closed? He pinched his nose with his fingers. He took another bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like almost nothing. Milan opened his eyes wide. "Dad! My strawberry got quiet in my mouth!"
